speechtext:
We are struggling now with a rather difficult economic period in our evolution as a nation. For too long we have been a nation that is top heavy with those who produce only services. Do hon. members know that today only one-tenth of the labour force is literally "carrying the can for Canada?" Do we know that the world is reallocating its trade priorities, that this global economic earthquake is rocking us to the very limits of our ability to pay for those goods and services we all think we cannot live without?
Even so stern a critic of the mining industry as former Premier Barrett of British Columbia, in a speech in my constituency last week made the alarming statement for him and exhorted that resource exploitation must now be undertaken. He was the premier whose deathless words, "leave it in the ground", are still well remembered in my province and are still ringing in the ears of others, in reference to minerals. Competition in copper from Chile is overwhelming. The attack in zinc, nickel and other metals is hurting our nation. All this reminds members that it is the primary producers of this country, the loggers, the miners, the fishermen and the agricultural producers who are so pitifully few in number, who literally support the rest of us.
The contribution made in Canada by the resource producers to the welfare of this country of ours is gigantic. We will together seek means of weathering this earthquake of the economy so that Canada can turn the corner once again to prosperity. However, in my opinion there will never again be the profits which were reaped so effortlessly in the fifties. They will not be realized in our time. 1 believe that in order to survive, we must be willing to make sure that not only do we survive, but the rest of the world as well.
I could not enter this debate on the Speech from the Throne without talking about reconfederation. There should be no losers in confederation. Our building of unity must be based on real values, not stereotyped ones. As long as one deals in stereotypes, tolerance and understanding are impossible. It is on the real and intrinsic value of each citizen that the strength of a nation can be reinforced.
We are the second largest nation in the world; our geography is overpowering. It has at times intimidated us as a people and it has deterred us from knowing our fellow citizens intimately. Until the banding of our nation by rail and by road, by radio and by television-and the task is still incomplete-we could perhaps afford the luxury of not knowing each other. No more. That which other nations may perceive as an economic burden of transportation and communication, we know to be a social necessity, linking together our people in a federation that takes into account our differences and our regional and geographic inequities.

When I came to Ottawa, I was often perplexed by continued reference to our country's five regions. My consciousness as a northwesterner turned the large end of the telescope on our own differentials and needs and, naturally, my five choices were, the Atlantic, central Canada, the prairies, British Columbia and the north. But here in Ottawa a central viewpoint from our national telescope showed the same malaise I had had, as I heard the regions solemnly named, B.C., the west, Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic, half an hour later in Newfoundland, with the north, if perceived at all, seen through the wrong end of the telescope by most everyday Canadians. This distortion, this telescopic myopia, is perhaps unavoidable in a nation where London, Ontario, is closer to London, England, than it is to Old Crow, and where it is cheaper to fly to Hawaii or the Caribbean for a winter holiday than it is to travel from Prince Rupert, my home, to our nation's capital.
Inevitably, there are forces, fed by the unique aspects of each region, which exert pressures on them to pull apart from the rest of the country. These pressures were what we overcame to create this Canada of ours. We must continue, both to respond to the pressure points and to resolve the legitimate grievances they spawn, in order to maintain and to improve the unity that we won through such effort over the last century. But we must address the issue on the basis of a united nation, not on the basis of six regions, each seeking to gain a better deal at the expense of the rest. "Balance-sheet" confederation has never worked, and it never will.
If we succumb to the forces that pull our regions apart, and neglect those that bind us together, we may well become, like Pirandello's characters, six regions in search of a nation, or like the blind people describing an elephant, with each defining, however he or she pleases, his or her own part of the beast, and with the additional burden of a tacit agreement that no line be crossed, that each remain within his or her own region and not "meddle" in the others' territory, while each seeks ever greater power and favour for that region.
It was this type of regionalism that led the premier of British Columbia to say, in 1872, when that province was still smarting over what were felt to be the inequitable terms of the Act of Union:
I would not object to a little revolution ... if after confederation we were treated unfairly.
This quote is from a truly unusual man, but perhaps an archetypal Canadian, a man from Nova Scotia, by way of California, named Bill Smith who so fell in love with the west that he changed his name to Amor de Cosmos, "lover of the Universe". But did his universal love include Canada? Looking backward in time it appears to be "cupboard-love" to me. But surely Amor de Cosmos was not alone then, and would not be so now, within confederation.
Small revolutions? There have been many of them. In fact, we are now in a time when psychologically we are six giant regions and numberless special interest groups waging small revolutions, based on sometimes real and sometimes suspected grievances that reflect the new reality in confederation. One hundred and ten years ago we were 4'A million people huddled
October 24, 1977

around the pivot points of Upper and Lower Canada like winterchilled children around a bonfire.
The fires are banked now and stretch from Newfoundland to the Queen Charlotte Islands, but our constitution remains geared to the bonfire rather than the solar cell. Unless collectively we have the wisdom to perceive the nature of a just and equitable reconfederation and to work continuously toward that goal, we will become fragmented into cultural, ethnic, linguistic, economic and geographic ghettos where regional self-interest, and "What's in it for me?" federalism saps the strength of our national union.
Listen to another British Columbia of early day, a "rentable federalist" of the same era as de Cosmos, John Helmcken, who on conversion to confederation several years after the Act of Union in 1871 said, "Love for Canada had to be acquired by the prosperity of the country and through our children."
"A Canadian is a Canadian, is a Canadian", the Prime Minister said shortly after Quebec made known its intention to secede from Canada. But who is this new Canadian? What is this larger Canada? We are a people who founded ourselves on an indigenous culture which we are only now coming to appreciate. The native people of Canada can teach us love of land and the warmth of sharing in a society that depends on each other in a co-operative manner. We are an officially bilingual nation, which does not mean every citizen must speak both English and French, but that every Canadian must be able to address the national government in his or her official language.
This government, unlike the opposition, does not regard language as a "divisive" force, but strongly and adamantly follows a policy of freedom of choice, genuine freedom of language choice as the only sensible policy. Canadians, too, are a polyethnic society where the best of each culture and of the past is nurtured and husbanded with devotion and retained as part of the fabric of this new Canada. Canada is a promise to the world. If we, with all our regional inequities, racial and cultural differences and political estrangements, can pull this grand diversity into an even greater nation, we shall have set the pattern for a global community that must inevitably follow.
Twenty-five years ago, in Prince Rupert, Prime Minister Louis St. Laurent said: "We shall never have real peace until the whole world becomes one large, good neighbourhood in which all men and women respect the rights of others and work together for the common good." We must remember that all men are our neighbours. As we, together, engage in this battle for our nation's future, I cannot ignore the heroic fight of the Fathers of Confederation 110 years ago to bring Canada into being. Some of their words still ring true today. I should like to quote from a speech made by Thomas D'Arcy McGee in Halifax in 1894. He said: "Who will oppose? Who are now opposed to the union? Only those who have a vested interest in
The Address-Mr. Brisco
their own insignificance." As a British Columbian, 1 say to Quebec:

Your presence is not without value for the future of our country. You are essential to its life and your presence is of absolute necessity.

Each person in this nation is the mother or the father of a new federation-a new and better Canada for all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to join in the debate on the Speech from the Throne. If the subject of part of my remarks is parochial, it is with justification. The federal government and the provincial government of British Columbia signed, in June of this year, a series of agreements. Indeed, two substantial agreements were signed under the DREE program, one dealing with industry and the other with agriculture.
It is interesting to note that in the subagreements, according to the terms of reference laid down by the governments themselves under the general development agreement for British Columbia, attention was paid to two or three areas which are closely spelled out. These areas which are singled out for special assistance are the northwest portion of British Columbia and the northeast portion of British Columbia. I have no quarrel with that; indeed, I think it is most commendable. But it is also interesting to note that the one area which is clearly identified in the agreement, but which has been totally ignored in terms of special consideration, is Kootenay West.
I must say that reading the industrial agreement I was amused and more than a little frustrated at the minister's definition of "small business". I know he is prepared to provide as a loan or a grant-it amounts to the same thing, because it is forgiveable-some $30,000 on the basis that the capital investment of the person making application for the money does not exceed $60,000. I would ask the minister responsible for small business, if he were in the House today-I see that his predecessor is here-whether, in his opinion, the $60,000 limit on capital investment can be considered to qualify under the definition this government has of small business. I am curious to know what, according to the colourful imagination of this government, $60,000 is going to accomplish. I suggest a person would have difficulty in establishing a Dixie Lee outlet or a Colonel Sander's chicken-stand with that amount of money, at today's equipment prices.
However, it is some comfort to us to learn that the Liberal caucus is visiting Kootenay West this weekend. I am encouraged by this, because as a result members may have an opportunity to grasp the problems they have ignored for the last 40 years. Perhaps they will learn for themselves about the rape they have imposed on Kootenay West with their Columbia River treaty. Perhaps they will get to understand the problems of Castlegar. Perhaps they will sit down with Audrey Moore. I hope they do. Perhaps they will ask her what she thinks of the DREE program and the amount of assistance likely to be forthcoming for Castlegar which is suffering from a serious water shortage.

October 24, 1977
The Address-Mr. Brisco
The government has told us it is seriously concerned about unemployment and that it wishes to support measures taken by industry to increase employment. Castlegar has within its borders a provincially-owned pulp mill and sawmill. This complex is now to undergo a $7 million expansion, which means additional jobs. However, there is no place where the workers may live, because any new homes which may be constructed in Castlegar today are built on the understanding that they will not have a water hook-up. The problem is that Castlegar, at the confluence of the Kootenay and Columbia Rivers, has to rely on wells in its own subsoil, and because of geographical configuration those wells do not draw water from the Columbia River system. They are wells whose content is highly alkaline. Instead of the soft, clean water which lies above the Keenleyside dam, the residents of Castlegar must put up with this system.
I urged the minister responsible for DREE to consider a subagreement similar to the one drafted for Fort Nelson, involving $3 million or $4 million-$7 million, as it was with Fort Nelson-federally, provincially and municipally shared. That plea fell on indifferent ears. They said, "We are coming up with a new industrial and rural agreement, and surely within this context there will be something for Castlegar". Officials of DREE have advised me that as far as they can determine, there is nothing in the terms of the subagreements which affects the city of Castlegar, even though there is a less than adequate supply of water through the hydrants for fire fighting: 50 per cent of the fire hydrants register less than 50 per cent of the required pressure.
Hon. members are aware, as is the minister responsible for DREE, that the Cominco plant in Trail is in process of a $435 million expansion program. That is more money than the federal government has ever spent in the riding in the history of Kootenay West. Here again, more jobs are being created and there is a need for housing. Because of its geographical position, there is no more room in Trail for houses to be built, so people are looking to Castlegar to provide the accommodation they need. The problem, of course, is that if they move to Castlegar, since no water supply is available they cannot build houses. If the government is going to put its money where its mouth is, if the government is truly concerned about employment and about human values in British Columbia, then when government members visit my riding of Kootenay West this should be the very first issue to which they address themselves.
One of the things I have discovered, to my despair, during the short interval I have been a member of parliament is the lack of social conscience on the part of the government. It really is not entirely the fault of government parliamentarians. Clearly, in my view, ministers fail to get the message across to senior civil servants, who have established their own little empires, that there is need for a heart and for sensitivity in government. How many members, Liberal, Conservative or NDP, have appealed to the minister of health in the past and said, "Mr. Minister, I have a senior citizen in my riding who has paid into the Canada Pension Plan for a number of years,

and when he applied for his old age pension he thought he was applying also for his CPP. After three months without his cheque, he discovered his mistake, and he is now asking to apply for his rightful benefits under the CPP and for the three or four months' lag in benefits which he missed because of his own ignorance"?
It is only recently that the minister, due to pressure from members on both sides, has at last amended the act to make provision for such cases. However, how many senior citizens have been robbed-there is no other word for it-of their Canada pension for a period of months? Because it was engraved in stone in some ridiculous government regulation, the minister was determined to stick to the book. How very unfortunate for Canadians. That is only one example, Mr. Speaker, of many in which the government has demonstrated its total lack of feeling.
If I had an opportunity to sit down quietly with some of my constituents, or indeed with all Canadians, I would say to them that one of the biggest frustrations I have today, as a member of parliament, is that some members of parliament have been dishonest and have deceived Canadians; that this government has on occasion demonstrated what can only be called corruption; that the government and its members sitting opposite, when confronted with evidence of corruption, of lying, of deceit and dishonesty, have jeered, hooted, howled, smiled and grinned at those who have with justification levelled charges.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, there are among us some who have a conscience. I find it very disturbing that a member would not accept with a great measure of seriousness the charges which I have heard levelled in the House in the past. But rather than accept those charges seriously, rather than expressing concern, they adopt a united front-the big grin, the deceitful laugh. I think Canadians are going to wake up somewhere down the line and realize just how dishonest this government has been, in terms of its dealings with the people.
So many examples have been raised before in the House of government arrogance, of the pork-barrel system. The Liberals laugh it off. What disturbs me most is that Canadians do not rise up in their anger and frustration and let the government know what they think of the blatant pork-barrelling of this government. One of the most laughable instances is the government's decentralization program. Let me refer to a Conservative riding, Cape Breton. One of the most laughable decisions of the government has to be the movement of the passport mailing office to Cape Breton. Quite frankly, I have advised my female constituents that the minute they give birth to a son or daughter they should consider making application for a passport, because it might just arrive at the same time as puberty of the child.

The community involved is Antigonish. Then the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) received some goodies for North Bay. The Speaker of the House had some goodies for Sudbury-and God knows

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am appalled, in the last week of the debate in which we have been participating, at the way the opposition has attacked the government without really any understanding of the kind of problems we are facing at this time. Also, I am appalled at the rather weak defence the government has made of a rather good record.
Before we talk about the problems of our time, we should look at the record of this government over the last ten years to see if its record is as bad as the opposition is saying it is. I can see it is much better than the government is declaring it to be. The most useful document I am able to acquire each year is the annual review of the OECD, the economic survey dealing with Canada. The books on this document were closed on June

30 and the document arrived in Ottawa some time in late August or early September.
I would like to refer to a few of the figures included in the document, to indicate the success this country has had relative to other countries. The OECD uses four indicators. They survey the seven major countries, of which Canada is one. This summit group representing those countries met in London. If the opposition had a chance, I suppose it would say Canada is seventh in that group because Canada has the smallest population and there is something wrong with that. However, we are part of that group of seven.
There are four indicators. The first indicator is real personal consumption. Canada leads in the group. The average annual increase for Canada over the period 1970 to 1976 is 6.5 per cent. Canada is first and the United States is fourth at 3.4 per cent. Another indicator is real disposal income per person employed. Canada is fourth in this category at 4.2 per cent. The figure for the United States is 1.6 per cent.
In total number of new jobs created, Canada leads the list with 3.2 per cent for every year, on average. Canada leads the seven countries in that category, with the U.S. second at 1.8 per cent. Let us talk about the increase in the household savings ratio. Canada is second and the United States is seventh. In these four categories which are used by the OECD-and we are talking about the years 1970 to 1976-we come first in two, second in one, and fourth in the other. Is that a bad performance? Is that an intolerable performance? Is that a mess? I say that is a fine performance, and I am critical of the government for not bringing this to the attention of the public.
There are a couple of other points which should be made with regard to this document. The document says that in 1974-75, at the cost of deterioration in the relative inflationary performance and the external balance because of this, Canada resisted the international recession much better than most other industrial countries. Following the shift in emphasis during 1975, which was a recession year, economic policy continued, in 1976, to give priority to reduction in inflation not only as an immediate objective but also as an essential condition for sustained improvement in output and employment. Those in the NDP said we should not have gone into controls; OECD said we did the right thing. We had the right priorities at that particular time.
In 1976, private consumption grew by 6 per cent in this country. Private savings also grew. The OECD says that this consumption did not grow because of any propensity to consume. In fact, the household savings ratio nearly doubled in the same period, but buoyant, real disposal income growth was achieved, thanks partly to an extremely rapid expansion in employment. That is why Canadians are better off, and to say that the government has not done these things is to miss completely the point of the OECD which, I assume, is a neutral body dealing with some 20 countries.
Let me refer to another figure, which does not come from OECD but from the Canadian Press of last week. Average family incomes, before taxes and deductions, rose by 5.9 per
October 24, 1977

cent to $19,110 in 1976 from $16,613 a year earlier. After inflation, that represents a 7 per cent increase in family incomes. Yet we put this forward and say that Canada is doing very badly.
In real dollars, since 1968-which was the year the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took the reins of government-that is, dollars which are not inflated by taking 1971 dollars as a constant figure, the gross national product increased by 42 per cent over these eight years. Canada's personal consumption- in real dollars, again-increased by 52 per cent. This, again, is from OECD.
Let us consider the clincher. Hon. members opposite say that the government is spending too much money and bankrupting the country. But personal income, in real dollars, increased by 52 per cent. Government expenditures-in other words, government consumption-increased by only 41 per cent, in real dollars, in that period. So are government expenditures in excess of personal expenditures? No. Personal consumption has gone up 15 percentage points faster than has government consumption. These are some of the things the government has not told the Canadian public, and I am annoyed that it has not. The reason 1 am annoyed is that I think it is unfair, in these very difficult times, to say that Canada has performed badly in the past eight or ten years, that it is all our fault and that it is only happening in Canada.
I have three major ideas I would like to convey in this speech, aside from getting the foregoing off my chest. I will be saying a great deal more about this as time goes on. The first point is that in a global sense there has been a great increase in the seriousness of problems which governments have had to face. Second, the institutions, the techniques and the means we have had at our disposal traditionally to solve these problems are not working. Third, there is a totally new element involved today with which we have not had to deal before, and that is scarcity of energy resources.
From these three points I would like to draw the conclusion that we have come to the end of an era, and that to get around the frustrations which are bothering all of us-the opposition, the government, and so forth-we have to take a new look at different techniques of solving our problems. I will not spend a great deal of time on the first two points, but 1 will try to illustrate what I mean in terms of inflation. For the first time in a non-war setting we have worldwide inflation which is serious. I understand that the summit group meeting last summer agreed that, generally speaking, 5 per cent must be a minimum inflation rate. In the industrial countries we have had an inflation rate over the last 100 years of between 1 per cent and 1.5 per cent. The rate went to about 2 per cent during the late sixties, and from 1973 on it jumped to 10 per cent and 12 per cent in this country and in other countries.
The summit group says that a 5 per cent basic figure is going to be common. That is the basic figure to work with, and there is very little we can do about it; we have to work with that figure. That is something we have not had before. I must remind hon. members that 5 per cent means a doubling every 14 years; it means that prices will double in 14 years, and in 28
The Address-Mr. McRae
years they will be four times what they are today. In 42 years they will be eight times what they are today, and so forth. It gets ridiculous. I am explaining this because I think it is important when we deal with energy growth.
There is a large unemployment problem all around the world. I am not just talking about Canada. For those who say that Japan has no unemployment problem, I refer to a couple of points made in the Globe and Mail last week. Only 8 per cent of companies recently surveyed expect any increase in permanent employment. Official statistics show that about one million people are wholly unemployed, but at least two million people are considered redundant by Japanese companies which are unable to dump them. In other words, workers are not fired in Japan; they are just made redundant. It is a kind of unorganized work-sharing. The article also makes the point that the Japanese stock exchange is very sluggish.
The New Democratic Party constantly assure us that everything that happens in Sweden is right. I should like to read a paragraph from The Economist, one of the best magazines in its field. I am not trying to show that Canada is worse, or better, but that the problem is global. Referring to Sweden, The Economist article reads as follows:
The picture is already bleak. The first half of this year saw Sweden's gnp falling (0.5 per cent) for the first time since 1945, and the total drop for 1977 will be 1 per cent-just as other industrial countries are averaging 4 per cent growth; unemployment (whether the visible 2.1 per cent unemployed, or 6 per cent total if those in subsidized employment or retraining are counted) is rising and inflation (prices are 14 per cent up on a year ago) is accelerating from 10 per cent a year-
This is in a country with a population about one-third that of Canada. The article goes on to say that subsidies to industries in trouble are gobbling up over $2 billion per year, and that the latest devaluation of the Swedish currency was 10 per cent. To say that Sweden, Japan, or any other country in the group I have mentioned, is doing better than Canada is ridiculous. I mentioned the indicators of the OECD. We are first in two, second in a third, and fourth out of seven in the fourth. To say that is a bad performance, or that Canada is in worse shape than other countries, is wrong.
All the industrial nations have the problems of inflation and unemployment, although to different degrees. Traditionally, inflation went up when unemployment went down, and went down when unemployment went up. But today inflation and unemployment are rising at the same time in all these countries. This is not the only area where we Find an increasing severe problem. We also find it in government spending. This year, we will have a deficit of around $8Vi billion and the Americans will have a deficit of about $60 billion. This is at a time of high inflation. That is another area we do not seem to be able to master.
At the heart of a lot of our troubles, and maybe at the heart of the situation in Sudbury, is the rapid rise in the size and power of multinational corporations. Several good studies have been done in the United States, particularly one by the finance committee of the United States Senate, which show that global

October 24, 1977
The Address-Mr. McRae
corporations control 1 Vi to twice the amount of the liquid assets of all the national banks of the countries they deal with. Control is not in the hands of governments-Swedish, Canadian, Japanese, West German, the United States-to the extent that it used to be. A good deal of it is in the hands of global corporations. We have a global problem of much greater magnitude than we had in the past.
The second point I should like to make is that our institutions are not working the way they should. Keynesian economics do not seem to be working the way they did. The New Democratic Party has taken a lot of swings at us for not putting enough demand into the economy. They say we only put a very small amount of demand into the economy by means of the last budget. Actually, we put $2.2 million worth of demand into the economy, in the budget as well as through indexing income tax, pensions, etc. It did not create as many jobs as they say the same amount of money will today. It is interesting that much of Canadian income today goes into savings-about five times as much as in the early 1960s. Therefore, if money is put out it does not necessarily go into demand.
We do not just face problems of economics today, but also social problems and stresses. In the community of Thunder Bay, for instance, there has been a great leap in adolescent problems in recent years. Perhaps that has something to do with unemployment, and so on. Recently, I attended a conference of the social planning council of Thunder Bay where the problem of adolescent social misbehaviour was discussed. It is interesting that during the whole evening only one mention was made of the school as an institution. People do not see the schools as the solution to their problems or as having any major effect in solving this kind of problem.
1 could go on talking about the fact that the institutions are not working and that we need new techniques, but I should like to deal with the third subject because it is one that concerns me even more than any others. I refer to the growing scarcity of energy resources. When I studied economics at high school and university, I was taught that scarcity was invented by bankers, and that if we could rid ourselves of the notion of scarcity there would be plenty for all. I grew up with the idea that there was nothing more sacred than an ever-growing gross national product; that whether you were a socialist or a capitalist did not matter-growth was what counted. Almost overnight-I have some thoughts on this because I think we were badly misguided-the world was told that there are shortages, that we are going to run out of energy, and that these shortages are going to produce some very serious problems. This is difficult for people to get used to. Have we been lied to, or is this the truth?
I have said in this House, in committee and outside the House, that the National Energy Board was negligent in not giving us fair warning of the danger. I have said it was negligence bordering on the criminal for not telling us long ago what the situation was. We are getting the figures today, but we did not get them in the past. I think this was gross negligence. I do not mind saying this outside the House, Mr. 
Speaker. I will say it anywhere, because I believe it and the figures will prove it.
There are all kinds of ramifications of the energy problem that we must face. We are told by the National Energy Board, and by a global group dealing with the problem on a global basis, that by 1985 Canada will have a shortage of oil roughly 25 per cent of our needs. The cost of oil alone will be about $6 billion. At present, 45 per cent of all the energy used in this country comes from oil, and 20 per cent from natural gas; so we cannot convert to something else very rapidly. A recent study by MIT indicates that this will be a worldwide problem.
We had some negative testimony, which did not refute the statement that I made in committee some time ago, that Saudi Arabian oil will probably run out in about 30 years' time. I made the statement which, again, was not refuted-that my son, who is now 15 years old, when he is my age, that is, 53, he will be living in a virtually oil-less world. The implications of that are horrendous in terms of the whole of our industry which is based on oil, such as the automotive industry, and so on.
There are alternatives, but they are not easy to achieve and they require a tremendous replacement of energy. The gas situation is not as bad, but we can expect a five or ten-year gap between gas and oil depletion. What kind of heritage will we leave to our sons, daughters and grandchildren? If this were just something I had in my mind, or something the National Energy Board had stated-as I indicated, the National Energy Board has not been too accurate in its predictions in the past- we could say, well, this should not be taken too seriously. But there are all kinds of other groups, such as the group which has put out the book called "Global Prospect" this summer, which say exactly the same thing, namely, that we have a massive problem.
The problem is not just in terms of scarcity of oil, but also in terms of scarcity of capital. I am told-I am not able to vouch for the figure-that the James Bay project is using up 50 cents of every capital dollar being used in Quebec today. The capital dollars that are badly needed in the pulp and paper industry to refurbish that industry, to make it more productive, are being used up in an energy project. When we talk about the future of energy capital growth-$180 billion over the next 15 years- in today's dollars, we are saying that 30 per cent, 35 per cent or perhaps 40 per cent of all the capital we will use in this country will be used for energy projects. That means there will be fewer dollars for consumer products. It means that a whole series of things will happen.
I would like to sum up some of these ideas because shortly my time will run out. First, there has been a quantum leap in the problems faced since the war-in the seriousness of problems facing governments. Second, the techniques and simple answers, about which I hear so much from the opposition and which I find so exasperating, are not working. The institutions we have are not working. For instance, some of our institutions have been bureaucratized to the point where they cannot work.
October 24, 1977

One of the reasons, I suggest, that the schools are not working is that they have become bureaucracies which have had to take on all kinds of other problems besides running the educational system. They have taken on the family, the community, and so on, and so they have ceased to function well. I am saying that our institutions, our techniques, the Keynesian techniques that we use, the social democratic notions that some groups use, are not working at this time and are not likely to work.
Third, we have an element of scarcity of energy in our industrial economy, which could be disastrous. From those three points 1 am led to believe, very much as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated two years ago this coming January, that we are coming to the end of an age, to the end of an era-an era that has been dominated by the notion of growth. This does not mean that we do not need growth, but we are rapidly coming to the end of this era, dominated totally by growth and in order to solve our problems we must look at new ways of doing things; we must adopt new approaches.

speechtext:
The frustrations which we feel in this House when we come together and shout at each other are caused in part by the fact that there are no simple answers to these problems. The techniques we have are not working.
I think that these frustrations will begin to go away when we start looking at new techniques. What are some of these techniques? I cannot tell you what the new world is going to be like, but I can tell you about some of the things that might happen and some of the things that might work. One of the things that will be coming into existence is a reduction in the size of things-the "small is beautiful" concept. The John Bullock independent business group is talking about this. They are saying that if you are going to be efficient, the best way is to be relatively small. This is not the total global picture, but it is one thing that I think will be there.
I think it will be terribly important that we develop into a conserver society, as opposed to a consumer society. We will still be consuming a great deal, but we must learn to conserve, to cut back on what we are using at this point.
I think we will find many people-1 found myself doing so this summer-returning to the land, returning to doing things oneself, returning to growing one's own produce, to using wood from the forest and food from the garden. This may sound fanciful, but in my community of Thunder Bay hundreds of people have moved to the country, to non-agricultural land, to good woodlots, beginning to cut down their cash flow requirements, to consume less and to conserve. Eventually, they will be living practically independently in terms of their economic needs.
We also have to look at-this will be the last point 1 will make in this respect, because my time is running out-some of the techniques which are not working in terms of creating employment. I do not believe, if we have a 6 per cent or a 7 per cent growth rate-we had one last year of 5 per cent-that we will be able to create the number of jobs that will be required,
The Address-Mr. W. Baker
given the degree labour participation in this country. We have approximately 300,000 people coming on to the labour market each year from schools as opposed to 60,000 in the 1950s. We will not be able to create enough jobs, even with a fantastic growth rate. So 1 do not think this is the solution in the creation of jobs.
There are two ways we can do it. One is to keep a certain group of society off the labour market permanently, which is one of the things we are doing now when we are saying the unemployment rate among our young people between 15 and 25 years of age is 12 per cent to 14 per cent. The other is to start sharing the work that is available among the people who are available to do the work. It seems to me that the Sudbury situation, which is a very grave one, has all kinds of ramifications.
We have here, essentially, a very strong case for doing some serious work-sharing. That work-sharing should involve three ingredients. First, it should involve a fairly large unemployment insurance fund which would be used in Sudbury, for example, to pay people who are not working. Second, it should involve a very big commitment on the part of INCO, perhaps refunding some of the tax already deferred. Third, there should be a sharing of work among the employees. I know many people in my community told me that, given the fact they have good incomes, they would prefer a four-day week, at the same hourly wage they are earning, than a five-day week. If one went to the individual workers-not to company representatives or union representatives-one would find many people in Sudbury who are well paid, who have a house, a car, a Skidoo-and will be getting a second Skidoo-who are beginning to think that perhaps their life would be better if they had more leisure and that work-sharing in the context of the three elements of industry, government and the worker, may be an answer to this problem.
I repeat what I said earlier. Is it much better to share the amount of work that is available among the people available to do the work, than have one group working for 40 years, eight hours a day and-

Mr. Speaker, I am always pleased to follow in debate the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae), whom I have always thought of as an optimistic member of this House who looks upon life in a

October 24, 1977
The Address-Mr. W. Baker
rather cheery way. However, if he was evincing the attitude of this country, more particularly within the ranks of the Liberal party, with regard to the future of this country, his solemn and somber attitude is something with which we should concern ourselves.
We live in a land that is replete with resources and a work force that has shown itself able to rise to challenges. If we must suffer under what he terms a conserver society, where we have to turn up our collars in the face of winds that are temporary, we are in much deeper trouble than we thought. I do not accept, and I hope others in this chamber do not accept, that the future of this country needs to be burdened with the sombre and doleful picture painted by the hon. member for Fort William.
Let us face up to a few things. In his speech today, the hon. member for Fort William said he was appalled at the weak defence of the government. Has it ever occurred to that hon. member that the government is defending weak case, not in terms of the ability of Canadians to come together and meet a difficult situation or crisis, but in terms of the government's involvement in it?
The hon. member mentioned the 1NCO case. That company, and indeed the whole of the mining industry in Canada, has become the handmaiden of the taxation policies of government. Governments have conveniently looked upon industry in Canada as the place from which they can soak up money with which to operate a whole host of programs. They did not think that when they are taxing and double-taxing, as they have done in the mining industry of Canada-and not just this government but other governments as well-they were removing from those agencies which employ thousands of Canadians their ability to function in competition with other nations of the world.
There are 21 nickel-producing countries in the world. If our taxation policies are so out of line that industries cannot compete-and that is the case with INCO-a lot of the blame must fall at the feet of the federal government as well as other governments. If that is to be the case, is it any wonder we are in trouble in competition in the world with respect to the production and sale of nickel?
What does the government do? Today, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) was asked in this House whether the government would consider taking leadership in terms of relieving the burden of taxation on this aspect of the mining industry. What did he say? He said the burden is a responsibility of the province, not his government. That is nonsense. The leadership, change and new approach which the hon. member for Fort William spoke about has to come from somewhere. I suggest the leadership should come from the national government of this country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I listened with great interest to the very eloquent and far-ranging speech made today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson). He said, as did the hon. member for Fort William, that when

we look at our position in relation to other countries, we should consider ourselves fortunate. Of course we should. However, that begs the question.
I would be the last to argue that, in terms of a nation which is just emerging in the middle of Africa, we should not consider ourselves fortunate, or in terms of some European nation that has been fraught with economic difficulties. What the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the hon. member for Fort William did not say was that we have moved from second place to ninth place in relation to all the nations of the world. While we can consider ourselves fortunate today, the question that must be in the mind of every Canadian is, why have we made that leap downward? Who was responsible for it? It was not Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, nor was it the New Democratic Party or the Social Credit Party. Those parties have not been in power in this country for ten years. It does not lie in the mouth of the hon. member for Fort William to make that assertion. What has happened is that there has been a failure on the part of this government properly to study or interpret what has been happening in the world; it did not relate its approach to Canada's economic policies in terms of other nations. There is a serious responsibility there which we should take. It does not help the fishermen, the INCO worker, the Newfoundland miner, the linerboard plant employee in Newfoundland, or the thousands of students and young people who over the past five years or more have come to me and other members of parliament, to say that we are as good, or better, than other nations in the world. That is a political cop-out.
The hon. member is correct in saying that we have to take some new approaches. We must look at the way our society is going, and ask ourselves whether we have now reached the point where we are asking too much of government. Is it the job of government to do things for you and for me, or is it the job of government to create an atmosphere where I can start doing things for myself, whether I am a farmer, a businessman or a teacher or whatever. It is not satisfactory to say that all countries have the same problems, because they do not. We have problems in Canada, in terms of our geography, which cannot be overcome by a minister simply making a speech in the House of Commons.
What has been the approach of the government with regard to this matter? Sometimes, in economic terms, in terms of gathering together the elements of this nation to face a problem, the government finds itself at odds with the facts.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco), who spoke a few moments ago, mentioned the whole problem of the decentralization of government. There isn't a person in the House of Commons who would argue that it is not a reasonable thing that elements of the federal government ought to be placed in various parts of the country. But no one in the House of Commons, surely-except, perhaps, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien)-would swallow the argument that decentralization must take place because it is going to help employment
October 24, 1977

in particular areas or because it is going to help national unity. Is our unity in this country so frail that the presence of a post office or an agency of government in a particular place is going to be the band-aid or an adhesive to hold it together? Of course not. No one honestly believes that.
This new program has been called expensive, in a period of restraint. It has been called a program of political patronage, and that is precisely what it is. We hear the argument that it is to help unemployment in those areas. What a silly argument that is. Look over the list of agencies which are being transferred. What are those agencies? Technical agencies, scientific agencies, specialized agencies. Are they going to lay-off the experts in these fields and hire others in the local areas? Of course not. They have sent 92 jobs to Cape Breton. The hon. member who represents Cape Breton called it a crumb from the table. Do they envisage that those 92 jobs will be filled down there? Of course not. Three quarters of the people are going to move down there at some personal and public expense and inconvenience. Less than 20 jobs will be taken through local employment in that area. This is the ridiculous part of the program, at a time of restraint.
What we face is a government which operates by cosmetics. Not too long ago, in the last session, I put a question on the order paper asking what studies had been undertaken with respect to the decentralization of the public service. I asked what was the cost per man-year and whether the government had done anything at all except canvas ministers to ask what agencies could be moved. Do you know what answer I received, Mr. Speaker? No studies had been carried out. It was pure politics. There had been no reviews, nothing. Yet they expect us to believe them when they say they are concerned.
In the week after the announcement was made, I had nine public services families come to my office saying, "Mr. Baker, I have a problem, my wife and I have a problem, our children have a problem. We have our aged parents settled here, and nobody told us we would have to disrupt our lives. No one ever told us we would have to sell our house and move somewhere else in Canada, however desirable that place might be. Nobody told us our children would have to interrupt their schooling and move from one province to another, with all the difficulties there are in this country with respect to disparity in educational standards. Yet we are forced to move, we are forced to go, by a government which has not learned the process of consultation."
Moreover, this is a costly process, Mr. Speaker. I believe the riding of the minister of the environment is receiving a scientific laboratory from the Department of National Health and Welfare at the cost of $7 million. The employees of the Department of National Health and Welfare have been told by officials of the department that it will cost about $7 million to move that laboratory, because they are not consulted very often. That is nonsense. They are consulted. A public servant who spoke to me about it said that right after the meeting there were five calls for information that was required immediately. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what would $7 million do to
The Address-Mr. W. Baker
build a sewage treatment in that area? A lot more than those jobs; a lot more than that government building.
The government has dealt into these issues in terms of cosmetics, and then they ask us to believe they are really serious and they know how to tackle the economic problems of the day. Of course they do not. The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) is in the House today. The hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) is here today. All of us, it does not matter where we sit, have had problems in terms of the public service. All of us have suffered from the tales told to us of the difficulties which have come upon public servants through the actions of a government which does not care. Every one of us has dealt with human problems as a result of the implementation of bilingualism in the public service. All of us know that careers have been wrecked. All of us know that the merit system had gone out the window. "Merit" is now a dirty word.
What does the government propose? It now proposes to change the policy, so that Canadians who have not had the advantage of growing up in a province where there are two languages spoken and where two languages can be learned, will be effectively barred from the public service of Canada by 1983. We have seen how the government deals with its public servants, how deputy ministers are prepared to go along with anything to satisfy the government, prepared to ruin the career of one man whose name I mentioned yesterday in the House of Commons, Mr. Sant Singh.
How will deputy ministers deal with the positions which are now to be filled on an imperative basis by bilingual Canadians, Canadians who are bilingual at the outset? Are Canadians not going to be given the opportunity of learning the other language? Moreover, Mr. Speaker, we are going to pay bonuses to people who have learned the two official languages-at least, they were supposed to-at public expense. How can any person look at this government and say they are sincere about restraint or about the public service?
Before this House resumed after the recess I called for an independent inquiry with respect to the implementation of bilingualism in the public service. I call for it again today. If the inquiries into the merit system which are going on in the public service with respect to the cost, the problems, the results, the cost-benefits of that implementation, are carried out within the service, then it will be a case of the government examining itself; it will be like putting a weasel in charge of a henhouse. Independence is what is required with respect to this matter.
Over the weekend the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talked about the protection of freedom in this country at a meeting of the rural lawyers of Quebec. He is a personable fellow, and they enjoyed the meeting. He said that in terms of language, which is a serious problem in Canada and which has been his preoccupation, to the detriment of Canada and in many other ways, the lawyers of this country should protect freedom, and one of the things he did not like about Quebec's bill 101 was the following:

The Address-Mr. W. Baker
We are forbidding French Canadian parents from sending their children to English schools just as 20 years ago Catholic parents were forbidden from sending their children to Protestant schools.
He said, further, that clauses of the province's French language charter which eliminate freedom of choice in language were "a step backwards for freedom". He told his audience that the documents which were produced by Mr. Gordon Robertson at his famous press conference, when he announced that the attack on lack of freedom would be no attack at all, indicated that the bill was reprehensible. It has been called a blot on the legislative landscape of this country. Yet what is his approach? His approach is to do nothing, to let somebody else carry the ball. "Never mind", he says, "I am the keeper of the constitution; let somebody else carry the ball". Never mind that owing to years of delay, feelings will develop in this country that will go a long way to destroy what feelings we have left for one another, which will drive us further apart. I think it is important, Mr. Speaker, that a government act. I think it is important that a government take a chance and go to court. I think it is important that a government do what it asks somebody else to do.
I met Quebec Protestant Home and School Association representatives in Ottawa the other day. They told me that in view of the educational limitations of bill 101, and due to its lack of courage, the federal government seems prepared to allow 1V2 million Canadians to rot, in terms of their place in society. The Prime Minister is absolutely right: bill 101 does deny French-speaking Canadians the opportunity to learn English. It also denies English-speaking Canadians in Quebec the right to use their own language as well as French.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) mentions the problems of the Inuit people. I understand an undertaking has been given that in that regard the James Bay Agreement bill would not be proclaimed. That undertaking was given in this House, and I intend to see that that undertaking-which was given to me in the House-is carried out.
There is not one member of this House who is prepared to take any step or to advocate any course which would mean the end of the French language or the French culture in Canada. I am sure there is no member who would want to advocate any course or take any step that would end the English culture in Canada or any other culture that goes to make up the Canadian mosaic. But surely the members of this House cannot sit idly by and in all good conscience approve a course of inaction in regard to the very important question of the right of Canadian parents to educate their children in the language of their choice all across this country.
I would be the first to say there have been differences of approach and timing in regard to the advancement of one province compared with another. That, of course, is wrapped up in the traditions of our country. I think it is improper, that it is really a false argument, to say that somehow British

Columbia, Alberta or Saskatchewan is wilfully deficient in educational terms, so far as minority languages are concerned, because their historical development has been different. But there will be no historical development at all if the government is prepared to sit back and to do nothing.
There are examples where governments have moved courageously and the country has withstood that move and has come to admire the government. But there is just no way that we can justify the stand that Quebec, or indeed any other province, shall not have special status, on the one hand, and then have a government, through a language paper, give it that special status.
The hon. member for Fort William spoke of new approaches that are required in the House in regard to financial control not just by the opposition but by the Parliament of Canada. We have a long way to go if we are to return to the House the opportunity of examining government programs and seeking information which the government relies on in advising itself. I would be the last to advocate that parliamentarians who are not members of cabinet should be privy to discussions which go on among cabinet members leading to a decision. On the other hand, I would be the first to argue that the House of Commons and the public of Canada, a pluralistic society in which we fund as well as promote interest groups, should be given information, points of view and expressions of opinion which are submitted to the government in arriving at certain decisions. 1 think we have to have that. If we do not, then parliament is going to act more and more on instinct rather than knowledge. In view of the complexity of government, this is precisely what is happening today.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) made a good speech in the House the other day, I thought, on what has happened within the bureaucracy, within the public service, and its attitude toward spending. When we examine estimates in this House, Mr. Speaker, we examine them piecemeal. We examine them in a way which actually pushes members of parliament into submitting that perhaps more should be spent on a particular program because it is a good one. But under our parliamentary system we have no opportunity today to examine estimates and government programs in a broad way. I think it is time all members of the House took a look at the machinery that it is necessary to put in place to enable us to contribute to a discussion of financial control over the expenditures of government. This has been lost to us, and should be restored to parliament. There is no machinery in parliament today which enables us to examine estimates in any way other than a piecemeal basis.
I put a proposal to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization in the last session of parliament. It was not taken up and it is still there. The hope was to give us an over-all review so that over the course of an ordinary parliament, Liberal, Conservative, New Democrat and Social Credit members would have an opportunity to examine a department's programs in depth in order to see whether Canadians are getting their money's-worth, to see whether a program is good, bad, or redundant and should be done away with. We do
October 24, 1977

not know this today; such decisions are made one way or the other in the bowels of the bureaucracy.
The bureaucrats are not bad people. They are not indecent people. They are not out to scalp Canada. They are humans, a group of human beings with a particular point of view. We must examine the procedures of the House whereby members, some of whom are very talented, can get themselves into the policy-making process. I recall the immigration bill regarding which options were considered in advance. Parliamentarians travelled the country hearing evidence long before any bill or regulations were drafted. As a result of this process there was a very short debate. A report was produced which to a great extent appeared in the form of legislation.
Too often in our system decisions are made by cabinet and the bureaucracy. When legislation reaches the floor of the House, the government has already made a decision from which it cannot move. As a result, debates in this House become long and acrimonious. 1 think that problem could be solved and many matters could be dealt with if we decided to change our approach. Many things can be done to deal with this question. We owe it to ourselves and our institution to make the change.
Mr. Douglas Fisher, in a column which appeared in the current issue of The Legion magazine which 1 see the hon. member for Ottawa West has in his hands-indicated that because of the complexity of our society, our institutions have not kept up. What has happened is that the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the chairman of the Canadian Radio and Television Commission, and the chairman of the task force on national unity, have become more important than this place.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the indulgence of my friends. 1 will not be too much longer. We have to look at our committee system in the House of Commons in a new way. There is one successful standing committee of this House, and that is the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. It is not successful because it is examining the Auditor General's report, but because it has attached to it a staff which is independent of the ordinary bureaucracy. It has attached to it a reputation of such high order that members on the government side do not choose to be partisan about the work of that committee. We should develop that approach in order to assist other committees. If our committee system is to function, then that must be done.
The Address-Mr. Hogan
There are a number of other requirements which I will speak about in due course. I do not intend to go further into that matter today, except to say that this institution of parliament will go further and further down in the estimation of the people of this country unless it can be given greater pre-eminence than the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or one of the joint chairmen of our national unity bureaucracy. speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in a famous 1975 end of the year interview with Carole Taylor and Bruce Phillips of the CTV, said the following:
Some economists say all you have got to do is get back to the free market system and make this market system work. It won't, you know.
But this same Prime Minister, in his economic lecture to members of the House on Wednesday, October 19, had an altogether different line. He had become converted to return to a free market to get us out of our increasing economic difficulties. He said that our prices are too high, and of course the markets of the world set the prices. This he gave as the major reason for our incease in unemployment which, as we know, is by far the highest of any country in the western world.
The serious decline of this country in recent years has been increasingly clear to Canadians and non-Canadians. To those of us who sit in parliament, the Prime Minister is seen as playing a sort of musical chairs with key cabinet appointments. This ultimately reveals the lack of a coherent economic philosophy for the nation. The country is economically stagnating and dangerously drifting, both economically and socially, under the leadership of the Prime Minister. Unemployment, inflation and a general environment of uncertainty is seriously eroding family and business confidence in the future of this nation.
The Prime Minister seemed to come to government in 1968, not only with a special style and charisma but with some sort of serious commitment to a "just society". This attitude has turned into a short-run, sort of seat of the pants, ad hoc reaction to the serious problems facing the nation. The Prime Minister's inconsistency is shown up not only in the general lack of an over-all consistent economic philosophy; it is personified and made clear in the speech he gave us in the House last Thursday, and it is also enshrined in the mini-budget of his new Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien).
Let us briefly review that mini-budget. The tax cut announced by the minister will take the form of an increase to $300, from $200, in the minimum amount of a federal income tax credit. It must be noted that this tax benefit will apply only to the current taxation year and will affect more than 7.5 million taxpayers. It is estimated to cost the government approximately $700 million in forgone income.
I think most economists would say that this provision will only be a modest stimulus to the economy. It will bring an
80025-13V4

October 24, 1977
The Address-Mr. Hogan
increased job-creation program which, along with the further $150 million approved for federal government works projects, will likely create between 30,000 and 40,000 temporary jobs. Given that more than 900,000 expect to be unemployed next year-and it could be easily one million-these programs promise too little.
Under the new mini-budget of the Minister of Finance, basic wage increases will be limited to 6 per cent for new wage contracts covering the coming year. If the government had not revised the wage control regulations, workers would have been entitled to claim increases of up to 8 per cent in the coming year. This cutback from the 8 per cent level to 6 per cent will, among other things, accentuate the squeeze on personal incomes and in turn that is bound to affect consumer spending and the national economy.
The Minister of Finance forecast that Canada would have an economic growth next year, in real terms, excluding inflationary pressures, of 5 per cent, compared with about 2 per cent this year. The effect on consumer spending by going from 8 per cent to 6 per cent, as announced in the budget, will make it extremely difficult, if not impossible, to achieve the 5 per cent real growth rate forecast for next year. We will be very lucky if our growth rate extends to 4 per cent. Given the new entrants into the labour force, the sluggish rate of growth in the economy in the last few years, and expected higher interest rates, we can expect very little, if any, relief for the crisis unemployment situation in this country.
Personally, I am scared that the tax cut announced will not result in as much an increase in spending as the minister had hoped for. Savings deposits at the national level grew by 19.7 per cent in the first quarter of this year, and are continuing at extremely high levels. It is more likely to be recognized as a transitory tax cut and much of it which will be applied to the middle-income earner will probably be saved and not entered into the income-spending stream. If the minister hoped that this type of stimulus would result in long-term increases in demand, which would in turn act as an accelerator for investment plans by manufacturers, he will be very disappointed. As is likely, a good part of the result of the tax cut will come out of current inventories.
The minister mentioned that about $1 million will be approved for an employment credit plan for private corporations. This would be a new approach to job creation in Canada, but this type of approach has been used in other countries. Such an employment tax credit program has to be carefully scrutinized because it is likely to give unanticipated windfalls to firms already planning expansion.
The other side of the question is that there is also danger that some employers will lay off initially too many workers at the time of any given cut-backs, only to hire them back again to take advantage of the employment credit plan. I would think that marginal corporations of medium and small sizes are unlikely to expand in the face of the uncertainties of rising inventories and costs. Experience of other countries has shown

that such a plan has not been nearly as successful as it had been hoped.
I am personally pleased that despite the fact that our devalued dollar is in large part due to a mismanaged economy, it will, however, continue to float. Certainly in the last several years our exchange rate has been somewhat over-valued. The continued floating of the dollar should have the over-all result of improving markets for domestically produced goods and a better market for Canada's exports. The price of some important inflation due to the higher price of imported manufactured materials and of consumer imports should be outweighed by the benefits coming from the improved employment prospect the lower dollar carries with it for domestically produced goods, and especially for Canada's exports.
While family allowances are still not indexed, income tax deductions for children under 16 will rise by $30, and for those over 16 to $60. The elderly and those with handicaps will receive an exemption increase of $100 to a maximum of $1,500.
I regret that the government did not see fit at this time to lift wage and price controls in Canada. They are obviously not a long term stabilizing influence on the economy, and the amount of short-term relief in terms of a dampening of expectations has been over-exaggerated.
The country has paid a significant cost in terms of uncertainties and of confrontation between labour, management, and government because of these controls. This, in my opinion, would have been a good time to lift them and to do it quickly and with a minimum amount of phasing out at a time when product markets, as well as labour and financial markets, are weak, and the danger of a post-controls explosion of prices and wages which would create a new round of troubles is at a minimum.
As it stands now workers will be forced to accept the maximum of 6 per cent wage increases when the consumer price index is going to run at 8 per cent or 8.5 per cent in the new year. That is asking for trouble and more confrontation. For the final few months of the existence of the AIB I ask this government to consider exempting the low income Atlantic region from AIB control.
This budget will do little or nothing for poor and low income Canadians whether they live in the Atlantic provinces, Quebec, Ontario, or any of the other provinces. There are not many people in Canada who realize that the lower paid 25 per cent of families in this country are only getting 4 per cent of our national pie, which we call the gross national product or national income, while the highest paid 25 per cent in this country are getting 42.2 per cent. How long do we have to tolerate this in a country which says it is committed to egalitarian principles and to bringing about equality with democracy? I would like to spend more time on this, but obviously, because 1 have only half an hour, I must move on.
In 1972 the then leader of the New Democratic Party, David Lewis, wrote a book which he titled "Louder Voices". In his book Mr. Lewis analyzed the tax treatment of corpora-
October 24, 1977

tions in this country in recent years, and concluded that it was grossly unfair. It was around this time that the now well known corporate rip-off concerns began to be expressed by our party. Over the post-war period the contribution of the corporate sector toward the financing of public services has considerably decreased in Canada. In 1950 personal income taxes contributed 20.3 per cent to total federal revenues, while corporate income taxes contributed 28 per cent. By 1974 personal income taxes were contributing 37.9 per cent of our federal revenues, while corporate income taxes were contributing only 15.7 per cent.
The essence of our argument, then-and it has not changed because the tax system has not changed, other than to increase corporate rip-offs-is that because of the great power and influence of large corporations, and because of the complexity of the tax system, a succession of federal governments have granted enormous concessions to big business, which have gone virtually unnoticed by ordinary people. We estimate the total annual value of these corporate incentives to be in excess of $5 billion per year, made up of roughly $4 billion because corporations are not required to pay current tax on their current incomes and $1 billion because of corporate rate reductions since 1972.
This is a serious problem for the people of Canada and for rational public policy because it means that a large segment of the government's discretionary financing decisions are not subject to regular scrutiny. Relatively few people are aware of the magnitude of hidden "tax expenditures" involved in the hidden corporate welfare system. Again, the United States- despite the many faults in its tax system-is well ahead of Canada in providing a public accounting of "tax expenditures." Every year a detailed summary of the cost of these tax concessions is presented to Congress.
In Canada no one has a clear indication of the precise cost of corporation tax concessions, apparently not even the federal Department of Finance. It is possible only to estimate the cost based on incomplete information which has been made available through official sources. In 1972 deferred income taxes amounted to $448 million in this country. In 1973 they went up to $959 million, practically a billion dollars. In 1974 they amounted to $1,468 billion. That is the last year about which we know. On that basis it is now believed by us, who have looked at the statistics and studied them, that the annual value of these corporate tax concessions is in excess of $6 billion, an amount equivalent to over 12 per cent of the 1976-77 federal budget. In other words it could be argued that the federal budget is really about 12 per cent higher than the figures which are printed in the annual public statement of the Minister of Finance.
Incidentally, the last available figures in the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act report show those corporation deferred taxes, which are in fact interest-free loans.
By way of digression, can hon. members imagine the average taxpayer, behind in the payment of his taxes to the Department of National Revenue, not being charged interest
The Address-Mr. Hogan
on his overdue current taxes? None of us could believe that, but it can happen with corporations.
1 started to say that the last available figures were for 1974. We can easily project for 1975, 1976 and 1977 that the total amount of deferred taxes for corporations operating in the Canadian economy is between $10 billion and $12 billion. When I hear the Minister of Finance say that he cannot give more income tax breaks to the poor or when I hear, as I did in the House today, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) asking the new Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) where she would get the funds for the beginning of a guaranteed annual income, the thought immediately strikes me-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I do not mind the hon. member making reference to me, but I think he should get his facts straight. I never asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) a question about anything. My question was directed to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) whose responsibility it is to save money. I was taken off guard when the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated she was prepared to look into the possibility of introducing a guaranteed annual income. As usual, the socialists really do not have their facts straight so I thought I should intervene to set the record straight.

speechtext: I suggest that is not a point of order, Mr. Speaker. If the hon. member did not ask the minister I mentioned, he asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) where they could get it.

speechtext: The hon. member is obviously against a guaranteed annual income.
