speechtext:
The thought immediately struck me, when I heard this question, that if our corporations, who have these billions of dollars of deferred taxes, were paying a market rate of interest to the government on them, we would have substantial funds to help the poor in a more serious way. Imagine if they had just had to pay 10 per cent on the $12 billion they now owe.
From the figures that I have seen, Mr. Speaker, the years 1973 and 1974 were some of the largest years from the point of view of tax deferrals granted in Canada since corporations were required to report these things. These, of course, were the years when the Hon. John Turner was the Minister of Finance and corporations like Canadian Pacific were allowed $56 million in tax deferrals. I cannot but wonder whether there is not a connection between Mr. Turner's incentives to Canadian Pacific and the fact that he is now a director of that corporation. As minister of finance he certainly showed himself as a great give-away artist to some of the large corporations. He might be forgiven, until you remember that, in order to defer taxes, you must have made a profit to have the taxes to be deferred in the first place. One wonders why the over $1 billion

October 24, 1977
The Address-Mr. Hogan
that was given to these corporations in the March budget, as well as all of these tax concessions that I have noted, have not ended up in increased plants and equipment and new jobs in the Canadian economy. One can only conclude that they were added to the cash flows of these companies and were probably used to buy the securities of other companies, and thus increase corporate concentration of wealth without adding much new employment for Canadian citizens.
There is nothing of specific help to the Atlantic provinces in the mini-budget despite the claims of the Prime Minister to the effect that we have received, over the years, large equalization grants, which is undeniable. Despite the effects of various federal regional bodies, from the Atlantic Development Board on through to DREE, there is not much substantial increase in earned per capita income in the Atlantic region. It is true that there was some improvement in the early years of the 1970's in per capital income which has largely been accounted for by increasing transfer payments from the federal government. We do not want more transfer payments, we want earned income. Our people want permanent jobs. They do not want to be continually saddled with high payments for unemployment insurance and welfare payouts.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And tax the corporations to death so that they cannot pay anybody.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
At a Department of Regional Economic Expansion meeting on April 7 I suggested that there is an especially severe disparity in the Atlantic region when you consider that the official figures of the 1971 census showed Sydney's per capita income was only 68 per cent of the Canadian average. For Glace Bay, it was 54 per cent, and New Waterford, in my riding, 48 per cent. Since the Cape Breton development Corporation took over the coal mines from Dosco-Hawker Siddeley there have been two major mine openings and substantial improvements to another major mine, No. 26 in Glace Bay, which produces coking coal which, even without washing, has about one to 1.1 per cent sulphur only. Yet the mines are still losing money, although Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), in his speech before the 29th Annual Convention of the Coal Association of Canada, at Edmonton, Alberta, on October 3, 1977 said:
It now appears that as a result of industry and government co-operation, and of new market and technological development, it will be possible to create an economically viable industry by the end of this decade... in Cape Breton.
Mr. Speaker, Francisco Parra, head of Petroleos de Venezuela, South America, in his speech before the Canadian Gas Association just two weeks ago said:
... in ten years the surplus oil production capacity of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) will gradually disappear as demand rises and additional supplies of oil from outside the OPEC area are not forthcoming in significant quantities ...
When this happens, international crude oil prices wilt again rise steeply, perhaps to as much as $20 a barrel in 1976 dollars.
This same theme has recently been reiterated by many experts on the oil industry, and even the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) reported it recently at a meeting in Paris. I want to suggest very strongly, Mr. Speaker,

that a mine started in 1978 in Cape Breton-Glace-Bay-New Waterford area would guarantee that Nova Scotia, which is so heavily dependant on imported oil, would have an assured source of supply and this would definitely guarantee that the Devco coal mines would more than break even from an operational point of view.
If you consider that at least one million tons of coal could be sent up from Sydney through the St. Lawrence to the southern industrial plants of Quebec, this country would literally save hundreds of millions of dollars in oil costs for an $80 million expansion for two new coal mines in Cape Breton. This would give us a total production of about six million tons, add directly at least 1,000 miners to that industry, and bring about an increase of at least another 1,000 jobs as spinoff. We desperately need these jobs, Mr. Speaker.
During the first quarter of 1977 for all of Cape Breton, including my own riding, that of the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir), and that of the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen)-who unfortunately has been sick recently and I wish him well-the government paid out $14.8 million, in round figures, in unemployment insurance. For the second quarter it was $13.3 million, for the fourth quarter $9.7 million, with a total payout to date for 1977 of $37,905,000. The number of unemployment insurance claimants in Cape Breton was 13,751 for January, 1977, and 14,221 in March, 1977. Unemployment insurance payments can go from $50 million to $60 million. We do not want that, Mr. Speaker. We want jobs. The jobs can be put there in terms of coal that is needed not only in Cape Breton and Nova Scotia but to offset the imported oil now being used by Abitibi and by cement and other industrial plants in southern Quebec. If money were invested in Cape Breton mines it would save this country millions of dollars later.
I do not pretend to have much expertise with regard to the fishing industry but I know that with all the good that the late Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson did for this country in trying to promote co-operative federalism, he was an over-zealous internationalist, and we in the Atlantic region have paid a price for that. The result of a policy of bilateral agreements with another country was that after 15 years we allowed foreign fleets to come into our waters and to take most of the fish. Mr. Pearson was too much of an internationalist and not enough of a nationalist. It is hard to fault anyone for being too much of an internationalist, but when your basic industry is allowed to deteriorate for 15 years, as was ours in the Atlantic region, one must call a spade a spade.
We are now turning a corner. I agree with the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) who is cautioning against too much development of off-shore fishing until more chance is given to different fish species to grow. It is true that he is considered in the Atlantic region to be too cautious, but I think that with proper planning the mistakes of the last 15 years can be corrected in the next 15.
October 24, 1977

What I am most concerned about is not only that our offshore fishing be assisted-because there is already a threat of a monopoly developing in Nova Scotia, a situation which I already brought to the attention of the anti-combines branch-but that inshore fishermen be assisted because they make up 90 per cent of all fishermen in Nova Scotia. We must make sure that these independent fishermen and smaller companies are protected and are given a chance to develop. The minister disagrees with me when 1 say that we need a 50 mile zone to protect our inshore fishermen, but 1 know, after talking with him, that he is reconsidering his view. I know there are difficulties between inshore and offshore fishermen on this score, but surely it will become increasingly clear, just as the minister said, that delineating a 200 mile zone across the Atlantic will not automatically result in the creation of a new offshore fishing industry. Neiiher will a 50 mile zone be a magical cure for the inshore fishermen. However, we are asking him to consider seriously whether this is not a sine qua non, a premise that must be accepted, if inshore fishing in certain areas is not to be completely wiped out, as threatens to be the case.
The only other point I would like to make in conclusion is that the Atlantic region especially, but the whole of Canada in general, needs more funding for transportation, particularly railway transportation. If we are to assume that the cost of oil will continue to increase and that gradually, in the next 30 years or so, our resources will be depleted, then it makes sense to put more money into the most labour intensive transportation industry. Railways do not use nearly as much energy as other forms of transportation.
Already the Department of Transport, the utilities in Ontario, the steel industry in Ontario, and the western premiers are getting together to consider whether or not to rebuild the whole railbed from British Columbia through Alberta to the terminal point of Thunder Bay, at an expenditure of some $2 billion in the next ten to 15 years. I suggest that the same thing should be done in the Atlantic region up to Montreal, and that over the next ten years we should put in $1.5 billion to help stabilize the rail plant in Sydney and the rail car plant at Trenton, Nova Scotia, which would have an important effect on the port of Halifax through the movement of goods to central Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first to commend the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Their responsibilities were attenuated since the speech as such is a summary of good intentions. What will be interesting is the forthcoming pieces of legislation.
In last Friday's issue of Le Droit, I read a comment from a journalist, Mr. Lacombe, who summarized his views more or less in the following words:
The Speech from the Throne: What Next?
To the extent that the Speech from the Throne informs us that the government's intentions are to improve the economic situation and maintain national unity, it is certainly a valuable document. To that extent, it is even a noble
The Address-Mr. C.-E. Dionne
document... Anyhow, it does not really matter and it is of little significance that the Speech from the Throne smacks of electoral opportunism, as many have said. What really matters, once again, is the work that will be done throughout the session which has just started.
Of course, that is what matters most. As other people, I have noticed that the speech often mentions the unemployment problem, and rightly so because this is the main problem Canada is faced with just now. I should like to quote a particular comment which I found most interesting:
The suffering which is currently the consequence of unemployment in Canada is seriously disquieting. It is neither fair nor admissible that so many men and women should be deprived of the dignity of gainful employment, and unable to meet their financial obligations and make plans for their future in a climate of confidence. It is not tolerable that so many people should be deprived of their rights to a useful and assured livelihood and that their families should carry the unfair burden of worries, uncertainties and deprivations. Unemployment is now, on a national scale, a very serious impediment to economic growth.
That is certainly a most beautiful way of putting it. However, I remember quite well that in its Speech from the Throne of February 27, 1974, the government stated:
Other measures will be taken to increase production and employment through providing workers with improved access to available jobs, and employers with improved access to Canada's manpower. These steps will relate employment policy, immigration policy and the activities of the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
In the throne speech delivered in 1972 which 1 have on hand, the following can be found:
Unemployment continues to be a matter of intense concern to the Government and will remain a primary focus of attention and action. Co-operation with the business and industrial communities will be extended even further to ensure a favourable business climate. As the economy continues to gain momentum, the private sector will be able increasingly to provide jobs for those Canadians.
Those years have elapsed and we are now facing conditions which I do not have to describe. Everybody is aware of it. The number of unemployed is gradually increasing and that is getting alarming. Yet our ancestors had to fear famines as a result of bad crops in some areas. They did not have the means of transportation we have. Today there is plenty, or there can be plenty provided we know how to use it. The forces of nature man has harnessed are multiplying goods while increasingly reducing his direct participation in the production process. Progress increases the number of goods while reducing the number of producers, and yet it is felt that only the producers should be entitled to the products.
It seems that since we get plenty with little work, man should have abundance while enjoying more leisure. Yet nobody has even found how to provide everybody with the necessaries. We have a long way to go. We have plenty in production but scarcity in distribution. Why? Is that a natural law? Not at all. That is not even a law, that is a convention set by men, convention which could do during centuries of labour and scarcity, but which can and must be changed to adjust the economic order to the present historical situation. That convention set up as a law by masters of money and profiteers of the system is running against the progress which it is deterring. It is inhuman because it makes man become the slave of money and keeps him in an unjustifiable state of deprivation.

October 24, 1977
The Address-Mr. C.-E. Dionne
It is the cause of both immense physical and spiritual sufferings. In a society which distributes its benefits to such an extent in proportion to work, the situation of the poor is both terrible and inexcusable.
In order to meet the difficulties faced by low-income people, we should first of all establish a plan which would guarantee them at least the minimum income above poverty level. No other measure is more urgent. It is unfortunate that no real guaranteed income program, no real legislation establishing the guaranteed income for everyone is put before Parliament. We have been hearing about this for 10 years or perhaps for more than this, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) sometimes suggests programs she intends to implement; this is a beginning but still far from being real guaranteed income legislation. This should exist in a country like ours which keeps pouring its wealth outside; I am not against this as I am prepared to help those who are in a difficult position, but we should be intelligent enough to organize here in Canada a system of life which would enable all citizens to look to the future with a little more confidence.
I will deal again with the unemployment problem since it was mentioned on several occasions in the Speech from the Throne. We have seen that after collating and studying various statistics on occasional, sectorial, seasonal and temporary unemployment, we now have permanent unemployment. Bill C-27 has been passed. It is a strange combination of commissioners, officials and consultants whose task seems to be a redefinition of duties and a reappraisal of the goals to get more jobs for Canadians. We wish good luck to all those who will assume administrative responsibilities in this combination. However, I am afraid this will not change the meaning of a number of provisions of the law as well as the regulations which the personnel of National Revenue, another group, use to disqualify unemployed people who experience problems with job insurability.
An employee is now required to pay back $2,500 to $3,000 benefits he has received. But the commission had found him eligible and paid him benefits.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: After he was found eligible!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, and after some kind of summary inquiry they decided to refer the case to income tax officials and told him: "This is unfortunate, but your job was not insurable, so you must pay back the overpaid amount."
Let us put ourselves in the place of the unemployed who, after receiving benefits because he was unemployed, is being asked by the commission to pay back. But here is something worse still. He should at least have been told after the first month so he could try and get welfare. But at that time he was eligible and he got the benefits. This is quite normal in view of current circumstances, but after one year he is told he had no right, he must pay back all that money.
I have cases in my office. Anybody can check them, I will be quite happy to show that this is absolutely accurate. I appeared many times before the Federal Court. Fortunately I met very sensible judges, including one of our former col-

leagues here, Mr. Justice Dube, who is now a member of that court. He realized by himself that this was unbearable, these jobs were insurable. A citizen from Saint-Jean-de-Dieu, a gentleman outside my constituency who comes to see me on occasion, was refunded $3,120 one month ago. He had been forced to borrow from his caisse populaire to survive after being denied unemployment insurance benefits because his job had been found uninsurable.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: This is senseless and should be changed. What with those irrational requirements about searching for a job, the unemployed worker should go on meeting serious difficulties. The unemployed is required to stay next to his telephone in case some bureaucrat in the manpower centre calls him. He is required to phone every possible place where some employer might need his services. He is required to go outside his community, otherwise he is told he is restricting his work opportunities to his community. He has to spend part of his benefits to move 25, 30 to 50 miles around his residence looking for non-existing jobs.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Even when they know there are no jobs!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, because there are civil servants at the manpower centre, good guys. There must be good workers among them; they are paid regularly for that. Now, in my area there are two or three manpower offices. Those people are there to make inquiries, to dig up information, to find out from the employers if jobs are available. The Unemployment Insurance Commission says: you must also go to the manpower centre. And if they don't go, then they are disqualified: You should have gone. And if the fellow says he did go, he is told that that is not enough, that he should have gone to see other employers. It just does not make sense.
Here is what goes on in my area, in particular, the one I represent here in this House. I quote, with some reluctance, an editorial published in my local paper, dated August 17, 1977. It is fairly recent, I quote:

speechtext:
He tries to make somebody budge so that people can earn their living in their own area. I quote again:
For almost a hundred years now several generations of young people in eastern Quebec have had to leave their own areas to seek elsewhere in Quebec, in Canada and even abroad, the employment from which depends their sustenance and their future.
In the last few years, in this area, in even larger numbers than ever before our educated youths have left school to find themselves in a regional labour market without any job openings. That also explains the fact that these young people must leave their homes in ever-increasing numbers to find employment.
We must stop a moment to look at the grim reality: the old saying that in our region a young man who wants employment has to leave has never been truer for our youth in eastern Quebec in 1977. Amazingly enough, such "institutionalized" emigration seems thus far to always have been accepted as an inescapable
October 24, 1977

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
phenomenon. The surest way for governments to fight that exodus from economically depressed areas would be the provision of financial and technical assistance to resource development cooperatives and other community development agencies which aim at fighting economic stagnation and enabling people to make a decent living where their roots are.
The foregoing article was published on August 17, 1977, in Le Saint-Laurent.
I wish 1 had more time available to me to put it all on the record, it is so interesting. Of course, one hesitates to try and really seek ways of curbing unemployment just because our system is faulty, our financial system is both corrupt and corrupting. When one tries to do something to curb unemployment one brings back inflation. So one is faced with two evil twins-unemployment and inflation. And the government, even if it is made up of a lot of intelligent people, at least people with big degrees, does not seem to find solutions.
The fight against inflation has resulted in increased unemployment. We were told, we saw, and we are told that controls were a lot more effective in controlling the salaries of workers than consumer commodity prices. That is so true that government jugglers are not thinking about ways of making the best out of a bad situation they helped create by preparing a period of decontrol.
That is playing with words, there is no doubt about it. About Bill C-27, I would like to point out, for example, that I find the amendments contained therein are reasonably based on common sense. 1 should have said Bill C-24, the Immigration Act. It gave the department the opportunity to announce that immigration would be better supervised to avoid the situation where new immigrants would contribute to increasing the rate of unemployment in Canada. It is a somewhat late decision but it is based on common sense.
There is another very important point I would like to make in this debate, and it has to do with working relations which are still very deficient. During the session just ended we had glaring examples of what we should never be forced to do. However, we did it. I am talking about the legislation to send striking workers back to work after passing legislation giving them the right to strike. Those are examples of flagrant contradiction that should be absolutely avoided. We should still have enough foresight to develop a rational allocation system for existing resources, without resorting to strikes when thousands of unemployed want to work.
The agricultural sector should not be neglected either. We know what has happened there in these past few years. I therefore draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), so he may use all means available to him to regularize a situation which is complicated by all kinds of jurisdictions, both federal and provincial. All kinds of things are happening but in the final analysis those producers whom the government once encouraged to produce do not receive the subsidies they can rightly expect.
Agricultural legislation oriented somehow or other, not always in the right direction, which resulted in an ever decreasing number of producers. Imposing a fine upon those who produce too much is not the best way to encourage
The Address-Mr. C.-E. Dionne production, at least I do not think so. There is a problem of distribution of benefits which should be granted to dairy producers. As a result of some jurisdictional disputes, a large number of producers who would otherwise be eligible are deprived of subsidies. This issue of legal difficulties should be solved, however so that those who have listened to government authorities asking them to increase their production become eligible.
I have also noted that the Speech from the Throne deals with an issue which is of great concern at present among the Canadian people-national unity. A lot of things were said in this regard and this issue is referred to on every possible occasion.

maintopic: EXODUS AND UNEMPLOYMENT NO LONGER TO BE ENDURED
speechtext: What is national unity?

maintopic: EXODUS AND UNEMPLOYMENT NO LONGER TO BE ENDURED
speechtext:
Of course, I, for one, would prefer the words "national harmony" but the fact remains that the Speech from the Throne deals with national unity. I will quote in particular this excerpt:
The government dedicates itself profoundly ...
Of course, the government is taking all the steps it can.
... to the re-discovery of the spirit of unity.
Can you imagine they do not even have any spirit of unity. It is essential and it is time to discover it.
It wishes to learn from all who are interested in Canada and who have thoughts on how it can be made a better place in which to live.
First, I would advise those who are looking for a spirit of unity to direct their research work to introducing legislation to allow the present generation of Canadians, who inherited from those who have colonized Canada and have given them the country they are living in at present, legislation that would allow them to live as heirs and not in debt as they are at present.
Following the political events of November 1976, the debates have too often concentrated on national unity. One should not forget problems like unemployment, inflation, even though I think this word has been coined to try and offer an easy explanation to financial difficulties. One should not forget all the other problems we face and engage in a debate with a government leader because of the elections of last fall, about which too many people have been uselessly seething with excitement. Let us establish a suitable legislation for Canada, and this problem of unity, of harmony will be automatically settled. When people are happy, there is obviously no trouble, but we must start our job so that Canadians can be happy in their country.
I think it would be wiser to pass legislation which would allow Canadians of each province to live like genuine heirs, as I said before, and I say it again, as genuine heirs instead of being constantly in debt, by the establishment of a fair sharing of the resources with which Canada is so generously endowed. History decided that we would live together on this territory. It is inconceivable that Canada, which is the product of a long lasting collective work, could go suddenly all to pieces. We can foresee occasional events which will prevent such a catas-
198

October 24, 1977
The Address-Mr. C.-E. Dionne trophe. The province of Quebec belongs to the whole of Canada, and Canada belongs to Quebecers as well as to the citizens of the other provinces of the confederation. Canada needs Quebec to keep its identity, and Quebec needs the rest of Canada to keep its own.
I shall close my comments with a brief passage from an article by Jean-Marc Poliquin published in the newspaper Le Quotidien of May 14, 1977, in which the author reported words spoken by Mr. Gordon Robertson during a speech before graduates of Dalhousie University in New Brunswick.
French Canadians will perhaps risk poverty to recover their dignity. A proud people cannot be bought-
I believe I still have time to express my convictions in these circumstances. I have followed as much as possible and as closely as possible the debates of federal-provincial conferences where people have always talked about the allocation of taxation powers. Finally, this is nearly always the subject that is discussed during those conferences.
I have here the text of the federal-provincial conference of January 14, 1941, I repeat, 1941! At that time, the British Columbia Premier, Mr. Pattullo, and I could mention premiers from other provinces, said the following:
Money, of course, is at the root of this whole question. While monetary measures should be based upon the productive capacity of our people, the productive capacity of our people can be amplified by wise monetary measures and other considerations.
Those were the words of the premier of British Columbia at the time.

maintopic: EXODUS AND UNEMPLOYMENT NO LONGER TO BE ENDURED
speechtext: Was he a Liberal, a Conservative or what?

maintopic: EXODUS AND UNEMPLOYMENT NO LONGER TO BE ENDURED
speechtext:
I think he was a Liberal.
I shall come back to a Social Credit premier of the time, because we must not forget that this premier, whose speech at the federal-provincial conference has already been quoted, Mr. William Aberhart, became premier of Alberta in 1935, in the middle of an economic crisis, at a time when a certain party made up the governments of all the provinces and of Canada. At that time they had no answer to give to those who wanted advice on various means which would help create new activities for Canadians. But the answer was always the same: not enough money. That had always been their regular response, their classical answer. The premier of the Province of Alberta used to say, back in 1941, talking about the British North America Act, as I stated before, that problems of unity, of harmony and diversity would quickly be solved if all Canadians could rest assured that they could live and shape their future according to their desires.
I will now quote you the remarks made by the premier of Alberta:
I do not believe that the British North America Act, or confederation, or whatever you like to call it, has been responsible since that time for the three D's which have marked the industrial history of some of our provinces-I mean, [Mr. Dionne (Kamouraska).J
decadence, debilitation, and death. I do not believe that confederation was the cause of these things, but I avow-
And at this moment he was addressing himself to the man who has always been the president of such conferences, namely the Prime Minister of Canada.
... sir, that something has been responsible for the awful plight that has settled upon the provinces. I notice sadly that the Ethiopian is still at large; the blight continues.
And he said further, and I quote:
Now, what is the job of each of us at this moment?
And at this point, I remind you that all the premiers of the provinces were together with the Prime Minister of Canada.
Is this conference a ration line, where we are to receive our dole, or is it a place in which each must grab all that he can to carry away with him? Is it not rather a conference to which we are privileged to bring, for the benefit of the Canadian nation, the combined gifts of thoughtfulness, wisdom, foresight, vision, tolerance and understanding with which we Canadians may be endowed?
Is this not our golden opportunity to lay the foundations for the never-before realized gifts of fraternity, freedom, equality of opportunity, and, what is also important, financial security? We are here, honourable chairman and gentlemen, I take it, to make it possible at some near future date to formulate for Canadians a series of decisions which will give them security in old age and the right to enjoy, according to their needs, the abundance of food and clothing and the comforts of adequate and sanitary shelter which the limitless resources of this great dominion can provide. We are here, I assert, to establish a heritage of education for those who seek to learn; of health for those who suffer pain or disease; of security and deliverance from debt for those who have built homes in their prime of life and who may face eviction and the loss of their sacred firesides when the lean years descend.
I conclude that quotation from the Social Credit premier-

We are here, I believe to draft a scheme of things for the Canada of the future, a scheme of things which will bring to that Canada a standard of justice which shall place human values above dollar values, a scheme of things that will provide for our fighting heroes when they return a standard of national viewpoint which shall not only recognize, as you have publicly stated ...

We are asked to make suggestions, to help rediscover unity. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to have the opportunity to participate in this important debate. First, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson) and the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Wood) the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I believe they have both delivered excellent speeches. They are very representative of their constituents and of this great country, Canada.

Although I could have spent the time allocated to me on broad national subjects, I have chosen instead to bring to the attention of this House, once again, the major concerns of my constituents on a local basis.

The issues of most concern to the citizens of this large constituency which includes about 50 municipalities from three provincial counties, Pontiac, Gatineau and Labelle, are related to the economy, and wherever they live, most of them are more interested in the possibility of job creation than in anything else. Certainly, they are concerned about the future of our province and of our country, but I am under the impression that the majority feels there are many things to be done in order to improve the living conditions. I should like, Mr. Speaker, to draw the ministers' and the members' attention to several questions of concern to this population.

The main concern over a large part of Pontiac in the last few years has been the future of Hilton Mines and its employees. This mine, which employed 350 persons at full
The Address-Mr. Lefebvre
production, has closed down its operations since this spring. Valiant efforts were made by a lot of people to find solutions in trying to keep the mine and mill in operation.
On March 27, 1974, when rumours of its closing became more and more numerous, I called a meeting to initiate discussion on the future of the mine and its 350 employees. This meeting was held in the county building in Campbell's Bay, and interested persons from the union, company, municipalities and the federal and provincial governments discussed the problem in depth. As a result two committees were set up: one to study industrial questions, and the other for manpower questions. Both these committees accomplished a great deal in bringing to both levels of government the facts and the seriousness of the situation. However, due to market conditions and cost of production, and in spite of many efforts made to find ways of continuing its operations, the mine finally had to close down completely.
All of us involved in the discussions which took place are of the opinion that the site on which the mine and the pellet mill are located would make an ideal site for an industrial park. The SAO, or Western Quebec Development Corporation, is preparing a report on this possibility. Being within an hour's drive from the Hull-Ottawa area, there is hope that new industries could be located there, helping to rebuild the economic base by providing job opportunities.
Modern highways and access roads for development of forest resources, tourism and other industries are of continuing interest. The citizens of the area are still waiting for the provincial government to decide finally to build a connecting road to link Pontiac County and Temiscamingue County. Many times in past years 1 have had opportunities to bring this to the attention of federal officials, including the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard). His department is ready to study a proposal from the Quebec government if it is presented under a federal-provincial program. I am sure it will be received in Ottawa with a great deal of interest. As everyone knows, the Canadian government could pay up to 60 per cent of the cost, if such a road project is put forward by the Quebec government on a cost-sharing basis.

The possibility of opening the Ottawa river to pleasure boats from Montreal to Temiscamingue is another project in which 1 earnestly believe, since a study requested by the hon. member for Renfrew North-Nipissing East (Mr. Hopkins) and myself has shown that such a project, once carried out, will have a tremendous economic impact in that region through direct job creation in the tourist industry and related services. People in that area have shown their support of and their interest in that project at three public meetings, and all municipalities, through resolutions, have supported my colleague and myself. I will pursue my efforts in that direction in the hope that the new Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) will also endorse such a project and that the specifications to circumvent the major obstacle between Lake
80025 - 14^2

October 24, 1977
The Address-Mr. Lefebvre
Deschenes and Chats Lake will be drawn up soon because it is the key to this whole tremendous project which, if carried out, would open a vast historical river to thousands of tourists who would like to explore it and holiday on its shores.
Mr. Speaker, the expectations of the people in the northern areas of Gatineau and Labelle were partly met when it was announced that the federal and provincial governments had signed agreements to improve the system of roads. There is no doubt that a modern highway from Sainte-Agathe to Abitibi, through the northern areas of Labelle and Gatineau, will have major economic effects, and this announcement might in turn generate a series of investments to create still more jobs. The announcement that an access road would be built between Temiscamingue and Maniwaki by the Ottawa and Quebec City governments, under a shared-cost program, has caused much enthusiasm, for this road will make resources more accessible and attract a greater number of tourists to a large area which is already famous for its lakes and forests. 1 suggest, however, that this road is but a link in the chain of similar roads which are most needed between the counties of Pontiac, Temiscamingue and Gatineau, which I have indicated to the Standing Committee on Regional Economic Expansion. We are counting on similar announcements within the next few years, so that the rural area on the Quebec side of the Ottawa River may finally be endowed with the installations which are necessary for its economic development; this area is rich in natural resources, and the projects which have been announced are the first of several for which the people had been asking for a long time.
In order to bring new jobs in that area, a lot of people are interested in the establishment of a federal penitentiary, and applications by Maniwaki, Grand-Remous and Mont-Laurier are now being considered by the Department of the Solicitor General of Canada. As you know, Mr. Speaker, 1 have taken personal interest in this matter for a long time and I agree with the fact that the establishment of such a penitentiary, with the permanent jobs it would create, would be very profitable to this area; if built, it would serve the whole Outaouais district, Abitibi and northern Laurentians.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Pacific made an announcement in May saying that they intended to ask the Canadian Transport Commission permission to abandon its railway service between Hull and Maniwaki and, a short time ago, the section between Sainte-Agathe and Mont-Laurier.
I immediately spoke against this and I am very pleased to see that the citizens in my area reacted at once through their mayors, aldermen, chambers of commerce, etc. I think that a lot of people will attend the public hearings in which the demands of the Canadian Pacific will be examined and that valid reasons will be put forward to prevent the abandonment of these lines. Instead of discontinuing its service, the Canadian Pacific should examine and find means to improve it. The citizens of this area feel that the Canadian Pacific has done nothing for years to maintain, improve or modernize its equipment and that this is why users become increasingly scarce. So we begin to have a vicious circle: less service, fewer users and

fewer customers, still less service until complete discontinuation.
The Canadian Pacific could also restore its passenger service in the area for people residing in the rural part of the Ottawa area and who go every day to Hull or Ottawa to work, with a service in the morning and in the evening and further trains on weekends for skiers and other sportsmen and for the numerous visitors.
This is not the right time for the Canadian Pacific to think of discontinuing its service but rather to think of offering an ever more efficient service to the people of this area, a service which meets the needs of modern life. These lines are very important. If they are abandoned, this will have very adverse effect at the very moment when economic development attracts more and more interests.

The need for more industry in this vast constituency is apparent, and I am happy that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has always studied with care the applications submitted by interested persons for grants. The area eligible for grants was enlarged during the past year, and new efforts are being made to enlarge it once again. DREE has played in the past and will in the future continue to play an important role in the expansion of job opportunities in this area.
Agriculture continues to occupy an important place in the economy of the region. More and more beef production is taking place, and there is a well established dairy industry supplying both industrial and fluid milk. 1 sincerely hope that the quarrels between Ottawa and Quebec on the hold-back of subsidies is solved soon. I do not believe the producer should bear the financial burden of seeing his payments lowered and millions of dollars being held in trust by the Quebec Federation of Milk Producers until the quarrel is settled. This is a constitutional question, and a way must be found to pay the producer the fullest amount possible until a solution to the question of jurisdiction is found.
Discussions are also taking place in various areas of the constituency as to the feasibility of establishing a slaughter house and sale barn so that local beef producers could have an outlet in their own district operated by themselves on a co-operative basis. I congratulate these people and, if plans do go ahead, I am sure officials of Agriculture Canada and DREE will listen carefully to any requests for aid.
There is great potential in the constituency of Pontiac for development in the fields of agriculture, tourism, forestry and industry. I will continue to support valid propositions to help expand the employment base in every section of Pontiac.
Earlier in this speech I mentioned the need for modern highways and access roads because they are very important to the future of my area. Hon. members will recall that in 1972 the NCC and the provincial government signed an agreement to upgrade all the highways in Quebec within the national capital region. Great strides were made in extending a modern highway 148 from Wyman to Hull and a new one from Hull
October 24, 1977

toward Wakefield on a shared cost program between the two levels of government. However, the new provincial government has blocked further construction of these two highways. I believe this is a backward step; everyone knows how badly they are needed. Over the years I have brought this need to the attention of the NCC officials many times, and no one applauded more than I did when the 1972 agreement was announced. I trust that the government of Quebec will reconsider this decision and that construction will start again soon on both of these important highway links.
Another program which has had great success in the area, Mr. Speaker, is rural RRAP, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, to upgrade the homes of residents of Canada's rural areas. This program, financed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation through loans and grants, has permitted the upgrading of many homes in the designated municipalities occupied by low and middle income families.
Not only are the homes made more comfortable and habitable, but jobs are created in the homes being repaired as well as in the manufacturing of building materials and sales outlets.
I trust that the government will continue this program until all the municipalities become eligible and have an opportunity to benefit from it.

Over the long term, Mr. Speaker, there are a whole series of projects that can help create jobs in that area. Over the short term, Canada Works Program, the LIP program, has had considerable success in the past and should again this year thanks to many projects from one end of the riding to the other. The millions of dollars recently spent have created hundreds of jobs while helping with the building of many community, municipal and other centres, and offering numerous services previously non-existent in those areas.
To hon. members who do not believe in those programs and who think that people are less interested in them, I should like to say that the second phase of the Canada Works Program has attracted this year more applications than ever before; at the present time, there are 151 applications for a total amount of $6.7 million though the budget for the riding has been set at $2.5 million only. Inevitably, many good projects will have to be turned down or cut down for lack of funds, despite the fact that the budget was increased this year to $2.5 million. Fortunately, there is a third stage and those who wish to make an application can do so until January 27, 1978.
These programs have a considerable effect in a rural environment and I congratulate the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) and the government for introducing them. I shall continue to support and defend them and I will do my best to make the minister more aware of the needs of the people of this riding.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the topics I have referred to in this speech demonstrate clearly that local people are concerned with a lot of projects. They are also concerned with the future
The Address-Mr. Jelinek
of their province and its position within Canada, but when one is looking for employment, one has understandably less time to think about the constitutional issue. Most are federalists and quite willing to settle the constitutional issue as soon as possible for it is obvious that the atmosphere created by the Parti Quebecois does not contribute to the discussions of industrial expansion or other matters.
I am not among those who think that separatists could disappear forever in a full employment situation, but the unemployed can wonder about their future in this country, Canada, and whether federalism is contributing to unemployments or if it helps in this regard. I am quite sure most of them feel it is helping a lot.

National unity, Mr. Speaker, is everyone's business and I encourage and applaud all those persons in my constituency who are participating in movements to promote it. I am sure we shall beat back the separatists, but vigilance is the password and every citizen must participate fully in the debates ahead.
Canada was founded by our forefathers with belief and trust; we must not let it fall by disbelief and mistrust. [Translation]
If Canada ever needed willing people who have confidence in their future, it is today. I am convinced that most Quebecers have such confidence and will do their duty for the sake of the future of a united country.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to add my name to those who have congratulated the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson) and the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Wood) on the capable manner in which they moved and seconded the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I should also like at this time to express my own appreciation, and I am certain I speak on behalf of my constituents as well, for the honour that Her Majesty bestowed on Canadians in general, and parliament in particular, by gracing us with her presence in our nation's capital during her Silver Jubilee Year and by so eloquently reading the government's Speech from the Throne.
Although the pageantry surrounding the Speech from the Throne is always exciting and most impressive, particularly with the presence of Her Majesty the Queen and His Royal Highness the Duke of Edinburgh, the intent and promise of the words cannot be taken seriously if based on former speeches under the jurisdiction of this administration. There is a sense that one has heard it all before. Indeed, when I witnessed the Speech from the Throne as a new member of parliament some five years ago, I was impressed and excited with the multitude of promises made and the many words exulting success and hope for Canada and Canadians in every field and every walk of life.

October 24, 1977
The Address-Mr. Jelinek
Unfortunately, my naive glimmer of expectation at that time was short lived and my hopes shattered as I quickly realized that what this administration outlined in the Speech from the Throne was merely a series of hollow words outlining false expectations of which very few, if any, were to materialize.
That Speech from the Throne five years ago was not an isolated incident. One can simply look at the record of subsequent Speeches from the Throne and budgets, as well as Liberal campaign promises, and conclude that time after time the present government has not lived up to its promises. It continues to make promises and continues to break them to the point of misleading the public. We do not have to go back five years in order to prove that.
I am sure all hon. members remember the last election campaign with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) swearing up and down that income and price controls were not an effective way to battle inflation, and saying that it was very wrong indeed of the official opposition to advocate a 90-day price control program. It should be remembered that it was a 90-day program we were proposing. After the Prime Minister received his mandate, overnight he saddled Canadians with the most stringent and incomprehensible wage and price controls program imaginable. In fact the government was so unorganized that it has taken over two years for it even to consider decontrols. Even today an aura of uncertainty exists in this regard. There are dozens, in fact hundreds of examples of unkept promises and examples of deceit by the Prime Minister and his government. Some of them, like controls, are premeditated indeed but, in fairness, I must also add that some are made, I am sure, inadvertently.
Members will recall the memorable occasion less than two years ago when the Prime Minister, on national television, told the nation in all seriousness, and I assume in good faith, that one of the main causes of domestic inflation was excessive government spending. He went on to outline a strict program of reduced expenditures by his government. People were happy to hear the Prime Minister taking government spending so seriously. Indeed, members on both sides of the House were pleased with the promises the Prime Minister made to the public at that time.
Unfortunately, once again this did not come out the way the Prime Minister promised. The government's budgetary deficit in the fiscal year 1976-1977 alone totalled $6.3 billion, a growth rate of more than 50 per cent over the previous year, hardly a figure reflecting the government's promise of restraint. Today the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) himself is unable to forecast an improvement in this regard, although the throne speech in a number of places makes reference to government restraint. A predicted deficit of $9 billion this year and $12 billion next year, a prediction that is made by the government itself, is not much restraint.
One can also recall the Prime Minister's famous phrase which has been repeated quite often but which I want to quote

again. This is what we are still talking about today. The Prime Minister said, "We will wrestle inflation to the ground". Not only has this not been accomplished, but indeed today our inflation rate is somewhere around 8,4 per cent and rising, far from the projected 6 per cent figure, which makes a sad commentary on the Prime Minister's famous quote. Now the Prime Minister has reversed his position and is blaming everyone but himself and his cabinet for the growing inflation.
The Prime Minister of any country must be trusted and respected when he comes out with statements, and the ones I have quoted are but a few of the kinds which our Prime Minister has been making. Limitation in time will not permit me to refer to all the unkept promises he and the Liberal administration have made over the past years, but it is becoming increasingly difficult for Canadians to trust and respect this Prime Minister after observing the record of his leadership. How can we respect him when recently, in reply to students in Toronto concerned about future employment possibilities in Canada, in a question and answer period-I am sure hon. members recall this-the Prime Minister said "If you don't like it here, you can leave the country and go elsewhere"? This country can no longer afford to have a leader of that calibre.
Let me sum up my feelings in this regard by quoting a recent editorial in one of Toronto's daily newspapers which concluded with the following paragraph. It is from an issue just last month. The paragraph reads:
The whole mess contributes to the conviction that Trudeau is the worst Prime Minister in our history and the person, more than any other, who is destroying Canada. He has to go-for the sake of our country ...

speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition does not whine, moan and blame the state of our economy on international forces or the lazy and lackadaisical attitudes of Canadians the way the Prime Minister does, putting the blame on everyone except himself and his cabinet. He, instead, continues to introduce realistic and positive programs which, if instituted, would reverse the negative trend that we have been living with in the past years.

This party has outlined its policies in all general areas, not only during this debate but over the past six to 12 months. Therefore, instead of repeating some of the policies that have already been dealt with by other party spokesmen-

If the hon. member opposite wants to find out what they were, he can read Hansard over the last week. He will find the policies in Hansard, especially those that deal with the economy.
Instead of repeating some of the policies that have already been dealt with by other party spokesmen, I should like to dwell briefly on a subject matter that 1 personally am responsible for on behalf of my party, namely, small business.
By the government's own admission, small business is responsible for 60 per cent of the labour force in Canada today. This obviously constitutes the largest potential employment sector by far, and therefore it is twice as incredible that no mention of this sector was made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) last Thursday in the so-called mini-budget, and only three words, Mr. Speaker, were dedicated to small business in the throne speech itself. That is a shame. It is a disgrace. It is an unfortunate situation as far as small business, which forms the backbone of our economy, is concerned.
With roughly one million Canadians unemployed, and with all indications pointing to an increase in this figure in the coming months, it is incredible that the government continues to ignore this vital sector which undoubtedly forms the backbone of our economic way of life. It is true that the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) inherited a ten point program from his predecessor which, after years of studies and consultations, generally concludes that the government should further study some of the problems related to small business.
I must give some credit, however, because this is the first time the government has ever given any indication that it knows small business even exists. However, further studies with no specific program is no help today. Studies and consultations have been made. The time has come for some positive and realistic incentive oriented programs.
Let me go to the ten point program that committed the government to continue to study, examine, and analyse specific aspects of small business. The points refer to existing programs, namely, Enterprise '77 and FBDB, and the tenth point which reads in part "efforts will be increased in order to make useful statistical information available" only adds to the already heavy paperwork burden imposed on small business by all levels of government-in short, Mr. Speaker, not one new point, not one new program; not one specific recommendation which would in any way, shape or form assist the already ailing small business community in Canada.
After studying that aspect for one and a half years, since the former minister was appointed to that position, even the government's own definition is vague and impractical. On the other hand we, in this party, after much consultation with small business representatives in every region of Canada, as
October 24, 1977

well as small business officials in other industrialized natfons such as the United States, Japan and West Germany, have time after time made specific and detailed incentive oriented recommendations in this House and elsewhere which, if implemented, would undoubtedly benefit the small businessman and therefore the economy as a whole.
I have given before, but allow me to put on record again and this time in point form only, some of the recommendations that we in the official opposition have been making for some time. I would like the new Minister of State (Small Business) to look at them and seriously consider their implementation in the very near future.
First, the definition is an important one. After studying small business administration around the world, we felt that the most workable general definition is that of the United States Small Business Administration which defines small business as an "owner-managed enterprise not dominant in its field". Further specific definitions can easily be outlined according to individual programs such as net worth, sales, number of employees and so on. We cannot have a general definition by number of employees like the government has recommended. What about foreign subsidiaries? What about small subsidiaries of large multinational corporations? They would fall within the small business definition. It cannot be.
Second, we would establish a small business secretariat which would function independently of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The secretariat's primary function would be to help small business cope with government and compete with big business. This the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce does not and cannot do. It is too big a department to oversee this very important segment of our economy. The secretariat would also put forward the interests of small business to other government departments and agencies, would assist small business with existing as well as new programs and cut through the existing maze of bureaucracy.
Thirdly, we would develop a small business act, a sort of unbrella act which would encompass all federal government matters dealing with small business and provide much needed incentive in the form of specific programs and/or commitments, such as some of the following. I realize I am repeating these, but some hon. members did want to know. Perhaps they do not read Hansard so I will give them the information at this time.
The first commitment would be (a) to change government tendering practices so that small business supplies a portion of government purchased goods and services. This is better known as the "set aside programs".
(b)	We would reduce considerably obsolete and/or duplicate form filling regulations, known as the "paper work burden". True, the government has taken some steps in this area, but not nearly enough. Small businesses are swamped with bureaucratic paperwork and regulations, and it is very possible to reduce, by at least 10 per cent for starters, excessive paperwork.
The Address-Mr. Jelinek
(c)	We would provide small business investment tax credits by giving a tax credit of up to $5,000 for capital investment in Canadian-owned small businesses.
(d)	We would provide assistance in the formation of small business export consortia-for obvious reasons.
(e)	We would remove the capital gains tax on transfers of a business from one family member to another.
(f)	We would encourage secondary manufacturing by way of tax and/or research and development incentive.
Secondary manufacturing in this country is far below its potential. It is an area where job creation possibilities are unlimited. It is an area in which we, as Canadians, have not even scratched the surface. It is a very important area.
We have also stated, Mr. Speaker, that we support in principle an employment tax credit, which in fairness I was pleased to hear the Minister of Finance touch upon in his speech last week. It is unfortunate, however, that even upon questioning he was unable to explain the government's proposal in this regard in more detail. One must only conclude that even the minister is not quite certain how this recommendation should be implemented. We certainly look to some form of legislation dealing with employment tax credit to assist in alleviating the unemployment crisis in Canada on a long-term basis, rather than continued handouts and give-aways which only create jobs for a temporary period of time.
Finally on small business, Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that last summer this House amended the Small Businesses Loans Act to increase the dollar value of loans as well as the aggregate amounts in the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. My seatmate brought this matter up with the Minister of Finance last week, who was not aware of the fact that we were promised at the time by the then minister of state (small business) that the new interest rates would be established, again by order in council, of course-what else is new with this government-within a short period of time, rates which would be pegged somewhere between 1 and 2 per cent above prime.
This is another unfortunate example of an unkept promise. Interest rates have not been established. The Small Businesses Loans Act, as a result, is in limbo and not being properly used across Canada by our chartered banks. We can no longer afford to wait. I repeat that realistic incentive oriented options must be made available immediately before it is too late. We are witnessing today more bankruptcies than ever before in the small business sector. The lack of specific government programs in this area is helping to create record levels of unemployment. Unless we act at once, I feel we could be witnessing the beginning of the demise of small business, and therefore of free enterprise as we know it.
This would probably not bother or disturb the Prime Minister too much, Sir, because you will recall that some one and a half years ago he indicated quite clearly in interviews that the free market system will not work. This demise is not because the free market system will not work, as the Prime Minister

October 24, 1977
The Address-Mr. Railton
tries to suggest; it is because he and his government will not allow that free market system the freedom to operate properly.
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not too sure that I was listening to a member of the House of Commons when the previous speaker began his venomous and virulent attack on the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), but I think probably the less said about it, the better. We should forget it.
It is gratifying to speak in this debate for a sentimental reason, namely, the fact that Her Majesty, as one of her Silver Jubilee official duties, graciously read the Address in the other place. Most Canadians are accepting the monarchy as a symbol of unity in this country and as a rallying point for our diverse Commonwealth. The force for good it maintains is largely because of the courage and concern our Queen displays.
I join, Mr. Speaker, with all members of this House in giving hearty congratulations to the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson) and the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Wood) on their eloquent and original orations in moving and seconding the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
As usual, Mr. Speaker, my contribution is a chance for me to give my own opinions on both constituency and national matters. Tonight I remind the House and Canada of their good fortune in having a Prime Minister who exhibits so much good judgment and clear thinking in handling the very difficult happenings in our nation at this time of crisis. His handling of our affairs is honest and courageous. Often at a cost in popularity he demands fair and just solutions to our economic and social needs, and he continually presses for true national unity. In his speech to the lawyers of Quebec he showed that Parti Quebecois policy is infringing not only on Quebec's English citizens' language rights, but also on the freedom of Canadians to live equally in, and to take part in deliberations in any part of, Canada. Thus the Parti Quebecois are restricting rights of Canadian citizens, in my opinion, unlawfully.
The new Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has gained stature by his strong and skillful defence of his "stand pat mini-budget". Mr. W. A. Wilson of the Ottawa Journal is
[Mr. Jelinek.l
rather chary of compliments, but he implied last weekend that the minister's speech was wise and statesmanlike. In these times when Canada has so much at stake, surely we deserve sane press writers and TV commentators like Wilson, people who will report all facets of news, good and bad, but mainly factual; people who will stop trying to make scare headlines and stop gloomy reporting. Most of us can do without their dubious help. We can work to turn petty catastrophies into triumph as our forefathers have always done. If the media are good citizens, they will turn their talents to positive thinking, as will our opposition in this House.
On that point, the official opposition seems to be satisfied to denigrate every good government effort. The NDP have been giving us superficial but so-called serious advice; however, Canadians know that we cannot spend our way out of unemployment. We know that to gain our rightful position we will have to work harder than ever before.
At this point I would turn from generalities to troubles we are experiencing in my own riding of Welland. Some of these exemplify social and economic trends in a wider context. To begin with, the electoral boundary commission mutilated the Welland riding and others to obtain one more needed seat in the Niagara peninsula, which now has five in all. Let me welcome these new electors right now to our new Welland riding. I am sure they will adjust and work for the good of their new constituency and the country. The commission could have found an almost painless solution to the problem but were completely deaf to the good suggestions from local interventions during hearings. To me there is something archaic about the idea of reviving three Commissioners every ten years just to have them impose completely autocratic decisions on the public. Surely, a local vote on alternatives would be a better way.
A happy conclusion to the abandoned canal crossing problem was achieved by the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan), and I thank him for it. Five million dollars was acknowledged to be a fair and just settlement.
The third bridge in Port Colborne is just a matter of time. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) accepts its need fully. He is negotiating with his counterpart in Ontario, but this should be completed soon. People will no doubt realize that the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority's policy is to abolish all overhead, bascule and lift bridges throughout the canal. This is the reason why the Port Robinson bridge was not replaced. A tunnel will be constructed eventually about half way between that community and Allanburg. There is some sense to the minister's asking that the federal contribution to the third bridge at Port Colborne be subtracted from the federal contribution to the tunnel in that city which will be built at a much later date.
Increase in Seaway tolls is the biggest controversial issue in my riding just now. The Chamber of Commerce, the mayors of St. Catharines, Welland, and Port Colborne, and the regional municipality of Niagara have taken a strong stand against the
October 24, 1977

move. They claim that the increases will be mainly on the Welland canal and will deter use of the canal. They claim that reduction in canal traffic is bound to occur with resulting depression to the Niagara area. The figures prepared by the Chamber are inaccurate and predicated on the prophesied drop in canal traffic. This drop will not occur.
Ships are now moving through the canal even when loaded at the ridiculously small fee of $100 per lock. These fees bring in $5 million a year and the operating costs are $20 million. The statement that the tolls could jump to $12,000 a ship is untrue. The very greatest would be approximately $6,000- and that by charging another one cent per bushel of wheat or another 47 cents on a ton of coal or ore. Freight costs for going through the canal would still be much cheaper than by road, rail, or via Atlantic or Pacific seaports. The United States government has been consulted and its studies are in agreement with ours. They see no reason to build a rival canal at a cost of two to three billion dollars. They intend to levy similar tolls soon on their own inland waterways.
On top of all this, people who complain that the government subsidizes other modes of transport should remember the following: rail gets a subsidy of five cents per mile, air receives two cents per mile. The government will now subsidize the Seaway by writing off the $625 million capital debt and the $225 million of back interest, not a bad subsidy! All the Welland canal portion of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority wants is to be paid its operating costs.
In the Welland riding, Mr. Speaker, unemployment has become a much bigger worry than last spring. Algoma Steel has closed its Port Colborne plant, and thus put 200 men out of work. Chances of reopening are not bright because of the softness of the steel markets in the world. This last week's huge INCO general lay-off was preceded in Port Colborne a month ago by the lay-off of 375 out of a work force of 1,300. My constituents feel that a great Canadian firm has become multinational and that its decision has been made outside Canada. They feel this firm has a responsibility not only to its shareholders but to the country whose natural resources and benevolent government assistance made its growth and developing success possible. We worry that this once Canadian company may gradually develop its foreign mines and plants and make the Canadian mines and plants completely unnecessary.
How can multinational companies be good corporate citizens? That is a question, with which INCO, the unions, and the federal and provincial governments are now wrestling. In spite of this concern, the idea advanced by the NDP to nationalize the nickel industry, would open the doors to many firms which are also struggling to keep their heads above water financially and encourage them to ask for the same treatment.
In the same vein, Atlas Steels of Welland has complained to the government, through me, that a stainless steel plant in Cuba is being built with Canadian government assistance and money as help to an emerging nation. If that is so, Atlas Steels rightly asks how we can build a plant which will be exporting
The Address-Mr. Railton
40,000 to 50,000 tons of stainless steel annually when it will be in direct competition with our own plant in Welland, especially when there is such a discrepancy in standards of living? Doesn't charity begin at home? I believe there is some gap in trade policy. I think we should look into the whole policy of funding low employment areas of Canada.
The three main concerns to which the Prime Minister addressed himself were unemployment, inflation, and national unity. Though the third affects the first two they naturally must, as a preliminary, be taken together. Without trying to be pedantic or authoritative still a few main points must be evident to us all.
Commodity demand has gone down and all markets are soft. Job creation at over 200,000 cannot keep up with the growth of our labour force which is the highest in the world, and which is due to the baby boom and ever-increasing female job participation. The rates in the Atlantic provinces and parts of Quebec are chronically very high. Ontario's rate is high; the west's is just barely acceptable.
Most people except unions and big business agree on the removal of AIB controls April 1, 1978. However, decontrols will be difficult and will require monitoring. They also require union and corporation co-operation with government. In my opinion these powerful bodies are not acting as good Canadian citizens, and public opinion should be directed at gaining their co-operation with government. However, our national unemployment figure may not go up much over 8 per cent, and inflation will stay near 7 per cent this year and should reduce by 2 per cent next year.
Last spring and winter, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Scarborough East Mr. (O'Connell) chaired a caucus committee on industrial policy of which I was a member and which I enjoyed tremendously. Among the speakers brought before us was a Dr. Smith, a vice-president of Toronto Dominion Bank, who foresees a continual annual growth of Canada's gross national product at 3.5 per cent. In the next 15 years he believes it will double, or increase even more. This means our foreign borrowing can be carried easily and still leave enough Canadian capital to develop our pipelines and energy strategy. With the exhibition of patience, we shall see this pipeline start in about a year's time. It needs to have political agreements signed, detailed planning and pre-start stockpiling.
The committee realizes that the old post-war easy prosperity is over for us and the whole group of western industrial nations. One of our industrial strategies should be for our branch plants to compete export-wise with their United States head office plants. Also, these Canadian branch plants must do their own research and development in Canada. Only by pushing our indigenous technology and know-how can we rebuild our export trade.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) stated last Friday that only half our citizens are willing to admit that an energy crisis is at hand and building up at a whirlwind rate. He clearly pointed out that the drain on world

October 24, 1977
The Address-Mr. Railton
oil supplies by western nations is increasing Third World tensions, which in turn places western democracy's future survival at stake. In Canada he calls for reduced energy use, conservation of energy, close supervision of all energy resources, more federal-provincial co-operation, and regulation of nuclear fuel. His department is spending large sums on solar and other renewable energy development. By 1990 he expects we will have spent $180 billion on energy programs.
The Prime Minister is criticized for calling on us to stop wringing our hands and to tighten our belts. It should be clear to all of us now that he foresaw the inevitable reduction in living standards and personal expectations, that we are trying to get more out of the economy than it can provide. We have concentrated on material possessions as a way to acquire happiness. More are now perceiving the old true values. People gain materially and become poor spiritually. The belt tightening experience will do us no harm. It will make us more conscious of our needy neighbours, our human brothers and sisters.
At this trying but challenging time in our history, Canadian unity is one of our greatest concerns. It seems strange that national sovereignty for the province of Quebec is being sought through separation, at a time when nationalism as a goal is recognized to be an ever-narrowing and unsatisfying pursuit.
