In spite of our difficulties, Canada has been doing very creditably in bringing social benefits and equal living standards to all parts of the country, in spite of their unequal resources, opportunities and haphazard development. Surely we all realize our country suffers from its northerly position, its huge size and its sparse population.
Quebec has received generous treatment from Ottawa. It is said that there are people in Quebec who harbour feelings of inferiority and hostility which really have no foundation in reality. Granted there are bigots in the rest of Canada who, just as senselessly, would let Quebec depart just to "serve them right". The three ideas consisting of total separation, sovereignty with economic association, or remaining in and participating in Confederation, if viewed logically, force us to admit that anything but full Confederation would lead to economic and political disaster, not only for Quebec, but also for all Canada.
The Parti Quebecois' unnatural hostility to the rest of Canada is even more regrettable when we see that the great multicultural group in Canada, which will soon be almost half our population, feels the need for Quebec's presence with us, just as much as do the greatest number of Anglophones.

Senator Maurice Lamontagne, in a speech at the University of Montreal on April 6, 1977, demonstrated that Quebec has at every turn since the settlement of 1763 been given greater assistance from the central government than her citizens received from successive provincial governments. He made a big point that French Canada was of so little interest to France after the battle of Quebec, that she chose Guadeloupe as a colony for its sugar, rather than accepting Quebec and fighting for the fur trade in Canada. He estimated that the French could very well have won this battle. Another big point he made was that by being an integral part of Canada, Quebec was saved from sliding helplessly into the American republic where its culture and language would have been lost completely.
There has been a fortuitous economic development in Canada up until now. Only by chance did Ontario develop steel and did Quebec go for textiles and shoes.
In spite of official Parti Quebecois dissent, most of us realize that Confederation has saved both Quebec and Canada. Both entities will continue to exist only through Confederation's continuance, albeit a confederation treated to constitutional reform.
Most Canadians-and this includes most Quebec Canadians-believe in a united Canada. They feel our country is unique and has something to contribute to world peace and understanding, simply by its continued existence after so much heart-searching dialogue. At this time we are encouraged by the speeches of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. They can promise this country not only a modicum of prosperity but also even a bright future. This will happen only if we relinquish our individual selfish patterns of action. In one or two years we shall turn that difficult corner in our history, but only if we are willing to work together as hard as our forefathers did to achieve Confederation 110 years ago.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this has been a very sad summer for Canada, and indeed it is going to be a very frightening and disastrous winter. There is no doubt about the fact that we are entering into a period in our economy when-

maintopic: EXODUS AND UNEMPLOYMENT NO LONGER TO BE ENDURED

maintopic: EXODUS AND UNEMPLOYMENT NO LONGER TO BE ENDURED
speechtext:
That has been said? I dare the government members to call an election. Anytime they want to call it, we are ready. They are not fooling the Canadian people for a single moment with the record they have put forward. By gosh, they do not even know how smart Canada is. Canada is ready for this election anytime they dare pull the plug, and so are we.
The last five years of the Trudeau regime have been disastrous. If you take an overlay of the record from indicators of the economy on unemployment, inflation, the devaluation of the dollar, the gross increase in taxation, and the government's take of the gross national product, and place it on to the period of time from 1962 to 1967 in Great Britain, you would have almost the identical pattern. The pattern shows that this country is on the same path Great Britain has been on, and look where we are today.
Hon. members opposite are scarcely worried that the government is about to go bankrupt. There are people in this nation who are full of imagination. We have people who are full of educated talent, but we have a government which will not give them encouragement to build a nation the way it ought to be built.
Our competitive advantage today is equal to the competitive advantage we had in 1969. We have to conclude that we have had a decade of waste. During the period from 1970 to 1976 unit labour costs in the manufacturing sector increased 49 per cent. In the United States they increased 28 per cent. We hear hon. members opposite regurgitating and uttering the excuse that all the nations of the world are having economic problems, that the United States dollar is being devalued and that U.S. unit labour costs are going up, but what hon. members opposite fail to recognize is that we are outstripping in a negative sense all our trading partners in the world. Relative to the United States, Japan or West Germany, we find that we are heading for economic chaos.
I remember as a child going to school being proud that our country, with only 20 million people and being the second largest nation in the world, had the second highest per capita income in the whole world. Since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came to power we are not even in the top ten. We have dropped from being something we could be proud of to the point where we do not even rank because of the economic policy of the government, which is not to care and the government will show people how to do things. As a result Canadians have lost incentive.
In 1969, the year after the Prime Minister took power, the Canadian hourly wage 65 cents lower than that in the United
The Address-Mr. Malone
States. Now, seven years later, our hourly wage is 64 cents higher than that in the United States. It is not a matter of right or wrong, because the rightness or wrongness of how much we are paid has to be relative to productivity. If we in Canada were producing more than our counterparts, we ought to be paid more. But the Prime Minister came into the House after the throne speech and admitted that it is a well documented fact that Canadian productivity is far below that of the United States. How in the world can we sell anything abroad if we charge more for our labour and, by the admission of the Prime Minister, produce less?
If the United States cannot afford to buy our products, who in the world can? We are in such a disadvantaged position on the international market that the government is looking for every avenue it can to hide itself from this economic malaise. To a large extent the whole question of national unity has been a government manufactured issue in order to hide its own faults with regard to mismanaging our economy in terms of the dollar, international trade and competitive advantage with other nations. To a large extent national unity would become a resolved issue if we did not have a million people in this country hunting for a way in which to earn their bread and butter.

government in a country with economic conditions like those which exist in Canada not even daring to introduce a budget? I think that is recognition of the fact that there is no leadership in the government. In the last election campaign the issue was leadership.
Recent Liberal budgets have been like a scavenger hunt. There have been no long-term policies and no indications of long term direction for the nation. The government has prostituted its citizens. I suggest that because it over-spends. The Prime Minister tells the people to practise restraint, but there has been tremendous growth in government expenditure and tremendous growth in the civil service. What a callous attitude this government has! The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) tells Canadians to spend more; the Prime Minister tells us to spend less; the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) tells us we have the strongest of all the economies in the western world. Whom in the Privy Council are we to believe?
When the Prime Minister took office in 1968, personal income tax represented 34 per cent of federal revenues. Today, 53 per cent of federal revenues come from personal income taxes. If the government is to be run on the backs of the people, the Prime Minister has no business telling Canadian citizens that they are the ones who ought to practise restraint, because that simply is not where the restraint is needed.
Everywhere we look there is waste without principle. The government decentralizes for the purpose of buying power, not for the purpose of helping the nation. The government sets up committees to study committees and to back away from the responsibility for its actions. There is no better example of that than the recent Hall Report. How tremendously discouraged Mr. Justice Emmett Hall must be at this time! He was asked to do a $1 million study, and then he found that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) set up another committee to study his principal recommendation. The Hall Report would not have been required if action had been taken after the Western Economic Opportunities Conference in Calgary in 1973. However, the Hall study was set up because the government would not go along with the recommendations of the Western Economic Opportunities Conference. So we had the Hall Report. Following that there was another committee to study it.
